     4	/-!
     5	# Games, tensor-product strategies, and value
     6	
     7	This file provides the finite game carrier used by the Pauli basis test.  Pure
     8	states are vectors in `EuclideanSpace`, and POVMs use the project's matrix
     9	`Measurement` structure.
    10	
    11	## References
    12	
    13	The source-facing nodes are `def:game`, `def:povm-conventions`,
    14	`def:tensor-product-strategy`, and `def:tensor-product-value` in
    15	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:47-82` and `8-26`.
    16	The paper origin is `references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:10-57`.
    17	-/
    18	
    19	open scoped BigOperators Matrix ComplexOrder
    20	
    21	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    22	
    23	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    24	open MIPStarRE.Quantum
    25	
    26	/--
    27	A finite two-player one-round game with a probability distribution on question
    28	pairs and a Boolean decision predicate.  This is `def:game` in
    29	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:51-59`, with paper origin
    30	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:10-24`.
    31	-/
    32	structure Game where
    33	  QuestionA : Type
    34	  QuestionB : Type
    35	  AnswerA : Type
    36	  AnswerB : Type
    37	  [questionAFintype : Fintype QuestionA]
    38	  [questionBFintype : Fintype QuestionB]
    39	  [answerAFintype : Fintype AnswerA]
    40	  [answerBFintype : Fintype AnswerB]
    41	  [questionADecidableEq : DecidableEq QuestionA]
    42	  [questionBDecidableEq : DecidableEq QuestionB]
    43	  [answerADecidableEq : DecidableEq AnswerA]
    44	  [answerBDecidableEq : DecidableEq AnswerB]
    45	  μ : Distribution (QuestionA × QuestionB)
    46	  μ_prob : μ.IsProbability
    47	  decide : QuestionA → QuestionB → AnswerA → AnswerB → Bool
    48	
    49	attribute [instance] Game.questionAFintype Game.questionBFintype
    50	  Game.answerAFintype Game.answerBFintype Game.questionADecidableEq
    51	  Game.questionBDecidableEq Game.answerADecidableEq Game.answerBDecidableEq
    52	
    53	/--
    54	The marginal of a joint POVM obtained by post-processing its answer pair.  This
    55	is the POVM convention of `def:povm-conventions` in
    56	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:8-26`; the post-processing operation
    57	is the already formalized `Measurement.postprocess`, with paper origin
    58	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:26-38`.
    59	-/
    60	noncomputable def marginalLeft {α β d : Type*}
    61	    [Fintype α] [Fintype β] [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    62	    [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    63	    (M : Measurement (α × β) d) : Measurement α d :=
    64	  M.postprocess Prod.fst
    65	
    66	/-- The right marginal of a joint POVM, obtained using `Prod.snd` in
    67	`def:povm-conventions`, `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:8-26`,
    68	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:26-38`.
    69	-/
    70	noncomputable def marginalRight {α β d : Type*}
    71	    [Fintype α] [Fintype β] [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    72	    [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    73	    (M : Measurement (α × β) d) : Measurement β d :=
    74	  M.postprocess Prod.snd
    75	
    76	/-- Projectivity of every effect in a POVM (`def:povm-conventions`, blueprint
    77	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:8-26`; paper origin
    78	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:68-72`). -/
    79	def Measurement.IsProjective {α d : Type*} [Fintype α] [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    80	    (M : Measurement α d) : Prop :=
    81	  ∀ a, IsProj (M.effect a)
    82	
    83	/--
    84	The tensor-product strategy of `def:tensor-product-strategy` in
    85	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:61-69` (paper origin
    86	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:26-38`).
    87	-/
    88	structure Strategy (G : Game) where
    89	  ιA : Type
    90	  ιB : Type
    91	  [ιAFintype : Fintype ιA]
    92	  [ιBFintype : Fintype ιB]
    93	  [ιADecidableEq : DecidableEq ιA]
    94	  [ιBDecidableEq : DecidableEq ιB]
    95	  ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA × ιB)
    96	  ψ_norm : ‖ψ‖ = 1
    97	  A : G.QuestionA → Measurement G.AnswerA ιA
    98	  B : G.QuestionB → Measurement G.AnswerB ιB
    99	
   100	attribute [instance] Strategy.ιAFintype Strategy.ιBFintype
   101	  Strategy.ιADecidableEq Strategy.ιBDecidableEq
   102	
   103	/-- The rectangular tensor placement used in strategy probabilities.  This is
   104	the finite-matrix realization of `def:tensor-product-strategy`, blueprint
   105	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:61-69`; paper origin
   106	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:26-38`.
   107	-/
   108	def heteroKron {ιA ιB : Type*} (A : Op ιA) (B : Op ιB) : Op (ιA × ιB) :=
   109	  Matrix.kronecker A B
   110	
   111	/- The Euclidean linear map is the shared action used by the value and distance
   112	functionals.  Keeping it at the Euclidean-space level avoids accidentally
   113	using the function-space supremum norm of `Matrix.mulVec`. -/
   114	/-- Apply a finite matrix to a Euclidean-space state.  This is the Hilbert-space
   115	action underlying `def:tensor-product-value`, paper
   116	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`. -/
   117	noncomputable def applyOperatorToState {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   118	    (M : Op ι) (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι :=
   119	  Matrix.toEuclideanLin M ψ
   120	
   121	/-- The Born weight of an answer pair for a strategy.  Lean-only support for
   122	`def:tensor-product-value`, blueprint `ch12_qpbt_games.tex:71-82`, paper
   123	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`. -/
   124	private noncomputable def outcomeWeight {G : Game} (S : Strategy G)
   125	    (x : G.QuestionA) (y : G.QuestionB) (a : G.AnswerA) (b : G.AnswerB) : ℝ :=
   126	  let M : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op (S.ιA × S.ιB) :=
   127	    heteroKron ((S.A x).effect a) ((S.B y).effect b)
   128	  let acted := applyOperatorToState M S.ψ
   129	  (inner ℂ S.ψ acted).re
   130	
   131	/--
   132	The tensor-product value, expressed as the distribution average of the Born
   133	probabilities.  This is `def:tensor-product-value` in
   134	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:71-82`, with paper origin
   135	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:40-57`.
   136	-/
   137	noncomputable def Strategy.value {G : Game} (S : Strategy G) : ℝ :=
   138	  avgOver G.μ (fun xy =>
   139	    ∑ a : G.AnswerA, ∑ b : G.AnswerB,
   140	      if G.decide xy.1 xy.2 a b then outcomeWeight S xy.1 xy.2 a b else 0)
   141	
   142	/--
   143	The tensor-product game value as a conditional supremum over all finite
   144	strategies.  The `sSup (Set.range ...)` form is the csSup formulation requested
   145	for `def:tensor-product-value`, blueprint
   146	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:71-82`, paper origin
   147	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:40-57`; attainment is
   148	intentionally not asserted here.
   149	-/
   150	noncomputable def Game.value (G : Game) : ℝ :=
   151	  sSup (Set.range (fun S : Strategy G => S.value))
   152	
   153	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

1	\section{Preliminaries}
     2	\label{sec:prelim}
     3	
     4	\paragraph{Notation.}
     5	We use $\Sigma$ to denote a finite alphabet.
     6	$\N$ is the set of positive integers.
     7	For $w\in\{0,1\}$, $\overline{w}$ denotes $1-w$.
     8	For $w\in\{\alice,\bob\}$, $\overline{w}=\bob$ if $w=\alice$ and
     9	$\overline{w}=\alice$ otherwise.
    10	(For notational convenience we often implicitly make the identifications
    11	$1\leftrightarrow \alice$ and $2\leftrightarrow \bob$.)
    12	We use $\F$ to denote a finite field.
    13	We write $M_n(\F)$ to denote the set of $n\times n$ matrices over $\F$.
    14	We write $I$ to denote the identity operator on a vector space.
    15	We write $\Tr(\cdot)$ for the matrix trace.
    16	We write $\mH$ to denote a separable Hilbert space.
    17	For a linear operator $T$, $\|T\|$ denotes the operator norm.
    18	
    19	\paragraph{Asymptotics.}
    20	All logarithms are base $2$.
    21	We use the notation $O(\cdot)$, $\poly(\cdot)$, and $\polylog(\cdot)$ in the
    22	following way.
    23	For $f,g:\N\to\R_+$ we write $f(n)=O(g(n))$ (omitting the integer $n$ when it is
    24	clear from context) to mean that there exists a constant $C>0$ such that for all
    25	$n\in\N$, $f(n)\leq C g(n)$.
    26	When we write $f(a_1,\ldots,a_k) = \poly(a_1,\ldots,a_k)$, this indicates that
    27	there exists a universal constant $C > 0$ (which may vary each time the notation
    28	is used in the paper) such that $f(a_1,\ldots,a_k) \leq C( a_1 \cdots a_k)^C$
    29	for all positive $a_1,\ldots,a_k$.
    30	Similarly, when we write $f(a_1,\ldots,a_k) = \polylog(a_1,\ldots,a_k)$, there
    31	exists a universal constant $C$ such that $f(a_1,\ldots,a_k) \leq C\prod_{i =
    32	  1}^k \log^C (1+ a_i)$ for all positive $a_1,\ldots,a_k$.
    33	Finally, we write $\log(a_1,\ldots,a_k)$ as short hand for $\prod_{i = 1}^k \log
    34	(1 + a_i)$.\footnote{The additional $1$ in the argument of the $\log(\cdot)$ is
    35	  to ensure that this quantity is strictly positive.}
    36	
    37	\subsection{Turing machines}
    38	\label{sec:tms}
    39	
    40	Turing machines are a model of computation introduced
    41	in~\cite{turing1937computable}, and play a central role in our modeling of verifiers for nonlocal
    42	games. Here we give an overview of certain aspects of Turing machines that are relevant for
    43	this paper. For an in-depth treatment of Turing machines, we refer the reader to the textbooks of 
    44	Papadimitriou~\cite{Pap94} or Sipser~\cite{sipser2012introduction}.

    32	/-- A formalization-only identity used to construct canonical line
    33	descriptions: applying the canonical line-representative projection twice has
    34	the same effect as applying it once. -/
    35	theorem lineRepMap_apply_self {K : Type*} [Field K] {m : ℕ}
    36	    (v u : Fin m → K) :
    37	    lineRepMap v (lineRepMap v u) = lineRepMap v u := by
    38	  simp [lineRepMap, canonicalProjOfKernel, LinearMap.comp_apply]
    39	
    40	/-- The two presentations of lines used by the low-degree question sampler. -/
    41	inductive LineKind where
    42	  | axis
    43	  | diagonal
    44	  deriving DecidableEq, Fintype
    45	
    46	/-- A seed-bearing line description for `def:line-point-dist`, blueprint
    47	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:85-95`, paper
    48	`08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:143-174,243-287`.
    49	
    50	An axis description stores its canonical base and seed. A diagonal description
    51	stores only the projected direction, together with its prefix-zero invariant.
    52	Both cases carry the assertion that their base is fixed by the
    53	appropriate `lineRepMap`. A value `j : Fin L.m` represents the paper's
    54	one-based coordinate `j + 1`. -/
    55	inductive LineDesc (L : LdParams) where
    56	  | axis (base : Fin L.m → ScalarQ L) (seed : ScalarQ L)
    57	      (baseFixed : lineRepMap (coordinateDirection (chiIndex L seed)) base = base)
    58	  | diagonal (base : Fin L.m → ScalarQ L) (seed : ScalarQ L)
    59	      (direction : Fin L.m → ScalarQ L)
    60	      (baseFixed : lineRepMap direction base = base)
    61	      (prefixZero : ∀ j : Fin L.m, j.val < (chiIndex L seed).val → direction j = 0)
    62	  deriving DecidableEq
    63	
    64	/-- The tag of a canonical line description. -/
    65	def LineDesc.kind {L : LdParams} : LineDesc L → LineKind
    66	  | .axis _ _ _ => .axis
    67	  | .diagonal _ _ _ _ _ => .diagonal
    68	
    69	/-- The seed retained by a canonical line description. -/
    70	def LineDesc.seed {L : LdParams} : LineDesc L → ScalarQ L
    71	  | .axis _ seed _ => seed
    72	  | .diagonal _ seed _ _ _ => seed
    73	
    74	/-- The canonical base stored by a line description. -/
    75	def LineDesc.base {L : LdParams} : LineDesc L → Fin L.m → ScalarQ L
    76	  | .axis base _ _ => base
    77	  | .diagonal base _ _ _ _ => base
    78	
    79	/-- The geometric direction represented by a canonical line description.
    80	Diagonal descriptions already store the projected data, so this map does
    81	not apply a second projection. -/
    82	def LineDesc.direction {L : LdParams} (line : LineDesc L) :
    83	    Fin L.m → ScalarQ L :=
    84	  match line with
    85	  | .axis _ seed _ => coordinateDirection (chiIndex L seed)
    86	  | .diagonal _ _ direction _ _ => direction
    87	
    88	/-- The canonical base is fixed by the representative map of the line's
    89	geometric direction. -/
    90	theorem LineDesc.base_fixed {L : LdParams} (line : LineDesc L) :
    91	    lineRepMap line.direction line.base = line.base := by
    92	  cases line with
    93	  | axis base seed baseFixed => exact baseFixed
    94	  | diagonal base seed direction baseFixed prefixZero => exact baseFixed
    95	
    96	/-- Every diagonal description carries the source prefix-zero invariant. -/
    97	theorem LineDesc.diagonal_prefix_zero {L : LdParams} (line : LineDesc L)
    98	    (hline : line.kind = .diagonal) :
    99	    ∀ j : Fin L.m, j.val < (chiIndex L line.seed).val → line.direction j = 0 := by
   100	  cases line with
   101	  | axis base seed baseFixed => simp [LineDesc.kind] at hline
   102	  | diagonal base seed direction baseFixed prefixZero => exact prefixZero
   103	
   104	/-- The point set represented by a seed-bearing line description. -/
   105	noncomputable def LineDesc.pointSet {L : LdParams} (line : LineDesc L) :
   106	    Set (Fin L.m → ScalarQ L) :=
   107	  linePoints line.base line.direction
   108	
   109	/-- Coefficient-list representation of a univariate polynomial of degree at
   110	most `c` over the scalar field of `L`. -/
   111	abbrev DegPoly (L : LdParams) (c : ℕ) := Fin (c + 1) → ScalarQ L
   112	
   113	/-- Evaluate a bounded coefficient-list polynomial. -/
   114	def degPolyEval {L : LdParams} {c : ℕ}
   115	    (f : DegPoly L c) (t : ScalarQ L) : ScalarQ L :=
   116	  ∑ i : Fin (c + 1), f i * t ^ i.val
   117	
   118	/-- Extend a coefficient list by zero from degree bound `c` to `c'`. -/
   119	def DegPoly.padTo {L : LdParams} {c c' : ℕ} (_h : c ≤ c')
   120	    (f : DegPoly L c) : DegPoly L c' :=
   121	  fun i =>
   122	    if hi : i.val < c + 1 then f ⟨i.val, hi⟩ else 0
   123	
   124	/-- A line polynomial evaluates to `a` at `u` when `u` has a line parameter
   125	and every such parameter gives the same value.  The universal clause handles
   126	the zero-direction presentation without choosing a sentinel parameter. -/
   127	def EvaluatesTo {L : LdParams} {c : ℕ} (line : LineDesc L)
   128	    (f : DegPoly L c) (u : Fin L.m → ScalarQ L) (a : ScalarQ L) : Prop :=
   129	  (∃ t : ScalarQ L, u = line.base + t • line.direction) ∧
   130	    ∀ t : ScalarQ L, u = line.base + t • line.direction → degPolyEval f t = a
   131	
   132	/-- Partially evaluate a line polynomial at a point. The value is undefined
   133	when the point does not determine an evaluation. This formalization-only
   134	completion is used in blueprint chapter 14; the displayed family at paper
   135	`14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex:197-206` has no bottom outcome. -/
   136	noncomputable def evalOpt {L : LdParams} {c : ℕ} (line : LineDesc L)
   137	    (u : Fin L.m → ScalarQ L) (f : DegPoly L c) : Option (ScalarQ L) := by
   138	  classical
   139	  exact if h : ∃ a : ScalarQ L, EvaluatesTo line f u a then
   140	    some (Classical.choose h)
   141	  else none
   142	
   143	/-- Convert an axis-line CL output to its seed-bearing presentation; paper
   144	`08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:243-257,276-287`. -/
   145	def aLineDescOf (L : LdParams) (line : LdSpace L) : LineDesc L :=
   146	  let direction := coordinateDirection (chiIndex L line.seed)
   147	  let base := lineRepMap direction line.point
   148	  LineDesc.axis base line.seed (lineRepMap_apply_self direction line.point)
   149	
   150	/-- Convert a diagonal-line CL output to its seed-bearing presentation; paper
   151	`08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:261-287`. -/
   152	def dLineDescOf (L : LdParams) (line : LdSpace L) : LineDesc L :=
   153	  let direction := prefixProjection (chiIndex L line.seed) line.direction
   154	  let base := lineRepMap direction line.point
   155	  LineDesc.diagonal base line.seed direction
   156	    (lineRepMap_apply_self direction line.point) (by
   157	      intro j hj
   158	      change prefixProjection (chiIndex L line.seed) line.direction j = 0
   159	      rw [prefixProjection, if_pos hj])
   160	
   161	/-- The axis-line/point component of the low-degree line-point sampler; paper
   162	`08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:243-257,274-287`. -/
   163	noncomputable def aLinePointDist (L : LdParams) :
   164	    Distribution (LineDesc L × (Fin L.m → ScalarQ L)) :=
   165	  (clDistribution (ldALineCL L) (ldPointCL L)).map fun sample =>
   166	    (aLineDescOf L sample.1, LdSpace.point sample.2)
   167	
   168	/-- The diagonal-line/point component of the low-degree line-point sampler; paper
   169	`08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:261-287`. -/
   170	noncomputable def dLinePointDist (L : LdParams) :
   171	    Distribution (LineDesc L × (Fin L.m → ScalarQ L)) :=
   172	  (clDistribution (ldDLineCL L) (ldPointCL L)).map fun sample =>
   173	    (dLineDescOf L sample.1, LdSpace.point sample.2)
   174	
   175	/-- The equal mixture of axis and diagonal line-point samples from
   176	`def:line-point-dist`; paper
   177	`08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:274-287`. -/
   178	noncomputable def linePointDist (L : LdParams) :
   179	    Distribution (LineDesc L × (Fin L.m → ScalarQ L)) :=
   180	  Distribution.mix (1 / 2) (by norm_num) (by norm_num)
   181	    (aLinePointDist L) (dLinePointDist L)
   182	
   183	/-- The affine line-point component has total probability one. -/
   184	theorem aLinePointDist_isProbability (L : LdParams) :
   185	    (aLinePointDist L).IsProbability := by
   186	  sorry
   187	
   188	/-- The diagonal line-point component has total probability one. -/
   189	theorem dLinePointDist_isProbability (L : LdParams) :
   190	    (dLinePointDist L).IsProbability := by
   191	  sorry
   192	
   193	/-- The line-point mixture has total probability one. -/
   194	theorem linePointDist_isProbability (L : LdParams) :
   195	    (linePointDist L).IsProbability := by
   196	  exact Distribution.mix_isProbability _ _ _
   197	    (aLinePointDist_isProbability L) (dLinePointDist_isProbability L)
   198	    (by norm_num) (by norm_num)
   199

130	  Let $u,v \in \F_q^m$.
   131	  Then for all $u' \in \line(u,v)$, we have that $\line(u,v) = \line(u',v)$.
   132	\end{proposition}
   133	\begin{proof}
   134		Fix $u' \in \line(u,v)$.
   135	  We have that $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$.
   136	  Let $a \in \line(u,v)$.
   137	  This means that $a = u + sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$.
   138	  We also have that $a = u + (s - t + t)v = u + tv + (s - t)v = u' + (s - t)v$,
   139	  so $\line(u,v) \subseteq \line(u',v)$.
   140	  A similar argument shows that $\line(u',v) \subseteq \line(u,v)$.
   141	\end{proof}
   142	
   143	We now specify a canonical representation of lines $\line = \line(u,v)$ as pairs $(u_0,v)$
   144	where $u_0$ is a \emph{canonical representative} of $\line$ specified as
   145	follows.
   146	Let $L_v^{\lnf}: \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with the
   147	one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$ (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical} for a
   148	definition of canonical linear map).
   149	Note that for all $u \in \line$, we have that $L_v^{\lnf}(u)$ is a point in
   150	$\line$.
   151	This is because since the image and kernel of $L_v^{\lnf}$ are complementary
   152	subspaces by definition (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical}), any $u \in \F_q^m$ has a
   153	unique decomposition $u = u_0 + u_1$ where $u_0$ is in the image of $L_v^{\lnf}$
   154	and $u_1 \in \ker(L_v^{\lnf})$, which by definition is the subspace spanned by
   155	$v$.
   156	Thus $u_1 = tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$ and we have that $u_0 = u - tv \in \line$.
   157	In particular, if $u\in \line$ then $u_0 = L_v^{\lnf}(u) \in \line$ as well. 
   158	Furthermore, since $L_v^{\lnf}$ is a projection onto its image by definition, we
   159	have $L_v^{\lnf}(u_0) = u_0$.
   160	
   161	Next, note that for any $u,u' \in \line$, since $u-u' = sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$
   162	it follows that $L_v^\lnf(u) = L_v^\lnf(u')$.
   163	Thus $u_0 = u_0'$ and this shows that $L_v^\lnf$ gives a means to compute a
   164	canonical representative of lines.
   165	
   166	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]
   167	  \label{def:line-representative}
   168	  Let $\line$ be a line in direction $v$.
   169	  A canonical representative of $\line$ is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   170	  \[
   171	    u_0 = L_v^\lnf(u)
   172	  \]
   173	  for all $u \in \line$.
   174	\end{definition}
   175	
   176	
   177	
   178	\paragraph{Question distribution.}
   179	We now present the question distribution of the game $\game^\ld$ as a typed CL
   180	distribution (see \Cref{sec:types} for the definition of typed CL functions and
   181	typed CL distributions).
   182	The type set $\type^\ld$ of the game $\game^\ld$ we use is
   183	\[
   184		\type^\ld = \{ \Point, \ALine, \DLine \}\;.
   185	\]
   186	The distribution over question types is uniform over $\type^\ld \times \type^\ld$. 
   187	
   188	We introduce the corresponding typed CL functions $L_\Point$, $L_\ALine$,
   189	$L_\DLine$ where the corresponding CL distributions $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$
   190	and $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$ implement the axis line-versus-point and diagonal
   191	line-versus-point distributions, respectively.
   192	The functions are parametrized by a field size $q$, a dimension $m$, and three
   193	complementary register subspaces $V_\xpt,V_{\coord}, V_{\dir{}}$ of some ambient
   194	space.
   195	The register $V_\xpt$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$) is called the
   196	\emph{point register}, $V_\coord$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q$) is called the
   197	\emph{coordinate register}, and $V_{\dir{}}$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$)
   198	is called the \emph{direction register}, respectively.
   199	We let $V$ denote the direct sum $V_\xpt \oplus V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$.
   200	We identify elements of $V$ as triples $(u,s,v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q \times
   201	\F_q^m$.
   202	
   203	Define $L_\Point$ to be the $1$-level CL function that projects onto $V_\xpt$: for every $(u,s,v) \in V$,
   204	\begin{equation}
   205	  \label{eq:cl-ptf}
   206		L_\Point(u,s,v) = (u,0,0) \;.
   207	\end{equation}
   208	Define $L_\ALine$ to be the following $2$-level CL function:
   209	\begin{equation}
   210	  \label{eq:cl-alnf}
   211		L_\ALine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{e_i}(u), s, 0)\ \text{for all } (u,s,v) \in V,
   212	\end{equation}
   213	where $L^\lnf$ is the linear function used to compute the canonical
   214	representative of lines (see \Cref{def:line-representative}), and $i = \chi(s)$
   215	where we define $\chi(s)$ to be the unique integer such that
   216	\begin{equation}
   217	\label{eq:chi-func}
   218		s = (\chi(s) - 1) \frac{q}{m} + r
   219	\end{equation}
   220	for some $0 \leq r < q/m$, and we interpret the field element $s \in \F_q$ as an
   221	integer between $0$ and $q - 1$).
   222	The function $L_\ALine$ is the concatenation of the $1$-level CL function that
   223	projects the subspaces $V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ down to $V_\coord$ (i.e.
   224	zeroes out the entire $V_{\dir{}}$ register), and the family of $1$-level CL
   225	functions $\{L^\lnf_{e_i} \}$ acting on $V_\xpt$, indexed by $i \in
   226	\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   227	(See \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation.)
   228	Thus $L_\ALine$ is a $2$-level CL function.
   229	
   230	Define $L_\DLine$ to be the following $3$-level CL function: for all $(u,s,v) \in
   231	V$,
   232	\begin{equation}
   233	\label{eq:cl-dlnf}
   234		L_\DLine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u),s,\pi_{i-1}(v))
   235	\end{equation}
   236	where $i = \chi(s)$.
   237	The function $L_\DLine$ is the concatenation of the following CL functions (again, see \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation): (i) the identity function on $V_{\coord}$ (which is a $1$-level CL function); (ii) for every $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ the $1$-level CL function on $V_{\dir{}}$ that maps $v \mapsto \pi_{i-1}(v)$ (i.e.~it zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of $v$), and (iii) for every pair $(s,v') \in V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$, the $1$-level CL function $L^\lnf_{v'}$ acting on $V_\xpt$. Thus $L_\DLine$ is a $3$-level CL function.
   238	
   239	
   240	The following two lemmas establish that the CL functions
   241	$L_\Point,L_\ALine,L_\DLine$ give rise to the axis-parallel line-versus-point and
   242	diagonal line-versus-point distributions.
   243	\begin{lemma}
   244		\label{lem:alnf}
   245		Consider the pair $(\line, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   246	  tuple $((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$,
   247	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,e_i)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   248	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a line that
   249	  goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \in
   250	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   251	\end{lemma}
   252	\begin{proof}
   253		Since $s$ is uniformly random in $\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$ by assumption, we
   254	  have that $i$ is uniformly random between $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and therefore
   255	  $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$.
   256	  Since $u_0 = L^{\lnf}_{e_i}(u)$, we have that $u \in \line(u_0,e_i)$.
   257	\end{proof}
   258	
   259	
   260	
   261	\begin{lemma}
   262		\label{lem:dlnf}
   263		Consider the pair $(\line,u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   264	  tuple $((u_0,s,v),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$,
   265	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,v)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   266	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a random
   267	  diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares the first $i-1$ coordinates
   268	  with $u$, for uniformly random $i$.
   269	\end{lemma}
   270	\begin{proof}
   271		The proof of this follows identically to \Cref{lem:alnf}.
   272	\end{proof}
   273	
   274	For later convenience we make the following definition. 
   275	
   276	\begin{definition}[Line-point distributions]
   277	        \label{def:line-point-dist}
   278	 The \emph{axis line-point distribution} $D_{\ALine}$ is the
   279	 distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$ over pairs $(\ell=(u_0,e_i),u)$
   280	 (we omit the $0$ elements for simplicity). The \emph{diagonal
   281	   line-point distribution} $D_{\DLine}$ is the distribution
   282	 $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$  over $(\ell=(u_0,s,v),u)$. The
   283	 \emph{line-point distribution} $D_{\Line}$ is the equal mixture of the axis-parallel line-point distribution and the diagonal line-point distribution.
   284	 In other words, a sample from $D_{\Line}$ is distributed as follows:
   285	 with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\ALine}$,
   286	 and with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\DLine}$.
   287	\end{definition}

    51	\begin{definition}
    52	Given integer $d,m$ and a prime power $q$ we denote by $\ideg_{d,m}(\F_q)$ the set of polynomials in $m$ variables
    53	  with \emph{individual} degree at most $d$ in each variable. When the field is clear from context we write $\ideg_{d,m}$. 	
    54		When
    55	  the number of variables is clear from context we
    56	  write $\ideg_d$. We denote by $\deg_{d}$ the set of polynomials with
    57	  \emph{total} degree at most $d$.
    58	\end{definition}
    59	
    60	Recall the low-degree code defined in \Cref{sec:ld-encoding}, in which vectors $h \in \F_q^\nqubits$ get mapped to polynomials $g_h \in \ideg_{d,m}(\F_q)$ such that for every $u \in \{0,1\}^m$, $g_h(u) = h_u$ where the coordinates of $h$ are indexed by binary strings of length $m$. For $x\in \F_q^m$, recall the definition of the vector $\ind_m(x) \in \F_q^\nqubits$ from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}. Recall also the finite field trace $\tr(\cdot)=\tr_{q\to 2}(\cdot):\F_q\to\F_2$, where $q=2^k$ for odd $k$, defined in Section~\ref{sec:subfields}. 
    61	
    62	
    63	
    64	Call a tuple $\omega = (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,r_\xpt,r_\zpt) \in (\F_q^m)^2
    65	\times (\F_q)^2$ \emph{anticommuting} if the quantity 
    66	 \[\gamma\,=\,\tr ((r_\xpt \cdot
    67	\ind_m(u_\xpt)) \cdot (r_\zpt \cdot \ind_m(u_\zpt)))\]
    68	introduced in~\Cref{eq:gamma-value} is not $0$, and \emph{commuting} if $\gamma=0$.
    69	
    70	\begin{fact}
    71	\label{fact:omega-anticomm-prob}
    72		The probability that a tuple $\omega= (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)$ sampled uniformly at random from $(\F_q^m)^2 \times (\F_q)^2$
    73		is anti-commuting is at least 
    74		\[
    75			(1 - q^{-m}) \cdot (1 - q^{-1}) \cdot \Big (1 - \frac{md}{q} \Big )  \cdot \frac{1}{2} \geq \Big (1 - \frac{3md}{q} \Big ) \cdot \frac{1}{2}.
    76		\]
    77		The probability that $\omega$ is commuting is also at least $\Big(1 - \frac{3md}{q} \Big ) \cdot \frac{1}{2}$.
    78	\end{fact}
    79	\begin{proof}
    80		First, note that $\ind_m(u_\xpt) = 0$ if and only if $u_\xpt = 0$. If $u_\xpt=0$ then $\omega$ is commuting. Otherwise, if $u_\xpt \neq 0$, then observe that for all $r_\xpt, r_\zpt, u_\zpt$,
    81		\begin{align*}
    82			\tr( (r_\xpt \cdot \ind_m(u_\xpt)) \cdot (r_\zpt \cdot
    83	                \ind_m(u_\zpt))) &= \tr( r_\xpt r_\zpt (\ind_m(u_\xpt) \cdot \ind_m(u_\zpt))) \\
    84									&= \tr( (r_\xpt r_\zpt) \cdot g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}(u_\zpt))\;,
    85		\end{align*}
    86		where $g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}$ is a nonzero polynomial in $\ideg_{d,m}(\F_q)$.
    87		
    88		If $r_\xpt = 0$, then $\omega$ is commuting. Condition on $r_\xpt \neq 0$.  Since $g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}\neq 0$ has total degree at most $md$, by the Schwartz-Zippel lemma the probability that $g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}(u_\zpt)$ is zero over a uniformly random choice of $u_\zpt$ is at most $md/q$. Conditioned on $g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}(u_\zpt) \neq 0$, the product $(r_\xpt r_\zpt) \cdot g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}(u_\zpt)$ is a uniformly random element of $\F_q$ when $r_\zpt$ is chosen uniformly at random. 
    89		
    90		The probability that $u_\xpt \neq 0, r_\xpt \neq 0, g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}(u_\zpt) \neq 0$ is at least $(1 - q^{-m}) \cdot (1 - q^{-1}) \cdot (1 - md/q)$ since $u_\xpt, r_\xpt, u_\zpt$ are chosen independently.
    91		
    92		Since $q = 2^t$ is an admissible field size, we have that for all $a \in \F_q$, the trace of $a$ is equal to $\sum_i a_i$ where $(a_1,\ldots,a_t)=\kappa(a) \in \F_2^t$ are defined in Section~\ref{sec:subfields}. Thus the probability that a uniformly random element of $\F_q$ has trace $0$ is exactly $1/2$. 
    93	\end{proof}

    95	In this appendix we often use the ``$\approx_\delta$'' notation to specify closeness of general operators (not necessarily POVMs) that are indexed by questions but not answers: given sets of operators $\{A^x \}$ and $\{B^x\}$ indexed by questions $x \in \cal{X}$, we write $A^x \approx_\delta B^x$ to denote \[
    96		\E_{x \sim \mu} \bra{\psi} (A^x - B^x)^\dagger (A^x - B^x)
    97	        \ket{\psi}\,\leq\, O(\delta)
    98	      \]
    99	where $\mu$ is a question distribution and $\ket{\psi}$ is a state that has been fixed by context. This will be useful for expressing closeness of observables, for example. The following two lemmas relate the closeness between sets of operators and weighted sums of those operators. 
   100	\begin{lemma}
   101	\label{lem:avg-closeness}
   102	Let $\{A^x \}$ and $\{B^x\}$ be operators indexed by some finite set $\mathcal{X}$, and let $\mu$ be a probability distribution over $\mathcal{X}$. Let $\{\alpha_x \}$ be a set of complex numbers such that $|\alpha_x| \leq 1$. Then if $A^x \approx_\delta B^x$ on average over $x$ drawn from $\mu$, then $A \approx_\delta B$, where $A = \E_x \alpha_x A^x$ and $B= \E_x \alpha_x B^x$.
   103	\end{lemma}
   104	\begin{proof}
   105	Expand
   106	\begin{align*}
   107		\Big\| \E_x \alpha_x \big ( A^x - B^x \big) \ket{\psi} \Big\|^2 &\leq \Big( \E_x \norm{ (A^x -B^x) \ket{\psi}} \Big)^2 \\
   108		&\leq \E_x \norm{(A^x - B^x) \ket{\psi}}^2 \\
   109		&\leq \delta\;.
   110	\end{align*}
   111	The first inequality is the triangle inequality and the second inequality is Jensen's inequality. 
   112	\end{proof}
   113	
   114	\begin{lemma}
   115	\label{lem:povm-to-obs}
   116	Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a finite set. Let $\{A^x_a \}_{a \in \mathcal{A}}$ and $\{B^x_a\}_{a \in \mathcal{A}}$ be POVMs and let $\{ \alpha_a \}_{a \in \mathcal{A}}$ be a collection of complex numbers on the unit circle. Let $A^x = \sum_a \alpha_a A^x_a$ and $B^x = \sum_a  \alpha_a B^x_a$. Then 
   117	\[
   118		A^x_a \approx_\delta B^x_a \quad \text{implies} \quad A^x \approx_{\delta'} B^x
   119	\]
   120	for $\delta' = |\mathcal{A}| \cdot \delta$.
   121	\end{lemma}
   122	\begin{proof}
   123	Expand
   124		\begin{align*}
   125			\E_x \norm{(A^x - B^x) \ket{\psi}}^2 &= \E_x \Big\|\sum_a \alpha_a (A^x_a - B^x_a) \ket{\psi}\Big\|^2 \\
   126			&\leq \E_x \Big( \sum_a \norm{ (A^x_a - B^x_a) \ket{\psi}} \Big)^2 \\
   127			&\leq \E_x |\mathcal{A}| \cdot \sum_a \norm{ (A^x_a - B^x_a) \ket{\psi}}^2 \\
   128			&\leq |\mathcal{A}| \cdot \delta\;.
   129		\end{align*}
   130	The first inequality follows from the triangle inequality, the second inequality follows from Cauchy-Schwarz, and the last inequality follows from the assumption that $A^x_a \approx_\delta B^x_a$. 
   131	\end{proof}

   134	The following lemma shows that POVMs that are approximately projective (in the sense of being self-consistent) are close to exact projective measurements. The lemma first appears in~\cite{KV11}; for a self-contained proof, see~\cite{ML20}.
   135	
   136	\begin{lemma}[Orthonormalization lemma]\label{lem:ortho}
   137	Let $0\leq \delta\leq 1$. There exists a function $\eta_{ortho}(\delta)\,=\, O\big(\delta^{1/4}\big)$ such that the following holds.  Let $\ket{\psi}$ be a state on $\mH_\alice \otimes \mH_\bob$ where $\mH_\alice,\mH_\bob$ are finite dimensional. Let $\{Q_a\}$ and $\{R_a\}$ be POVM on $\mH_\alice$ and $\mH_\bob$ respectively such that 
   138	\begin{equation}\label{eq:cons-cond} 
   139	Q_a \abc R_a \,.
   140	\end{equation}
   141	Then there exists a projective measurement $\{P_a\}$ such that
   142	\begin{equation}\label{eq:cons-ccl}
   143	  P_a \otimes \Id_\bob \,\approx_{\eta_{ortho}} Q_a \otimes \Id_\bob \;.
   144	\end{equation}
   145	\end{lemma}

   158	\label{sec:commutation}
   159	
   160	  Let $\qldparams = (q,m,d)$ be an admissible parameter tuple (Definition~\ref{def:admissible}) and let
   161	  $\strategy = (\ket{\psi},M)$ be a strategy for
   162	  $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ that succeeds with probability at least $1 - \eps$, where $\ket{\psi}$ is a bipartite state on registers $\alice$ and $\bob$, with associated Hilbert spaces $\mH_\alice$ and $\mH_\bob$ respectively. For notational convenience we use $M$ to denote the operators for both players; it will be clear from context which player's operators we are referring to (for example, we write $M^{(\Point,W),u}_a \otimes \Id_\bob$ to indicate that $M^{(\Point,W),u}_a$ is viewed as an operator acting on register $\alice$).
   163	  
   164	  Using Naimark's
   165	  theorem (as formulated in~\cite[Theorem 5.1]{ML20}), at the cost of
   166	  extending the state $\ket{\psi}$ by adding sufficiently many qubits
   167	  initialized in the $\ket{0}$ state we may assume
   168	  that the measurements in $\strategy$ are projective. Let
   169	  \[ \ket{\psi'} = (\ket{\psi} \otimes \ket{0 \cdots 0} \otimes \ket{0
   170	      \cdots 0})_{\alice \bob} \]
   171	  be the extended state. In the remainder of this section, we
   172	  will work with the projective strategy on the extended state, which we continue labeling $\ket{\psi}$ (instead of $\ket{\psi'}$) for notational convenience.
   173	
   174	We introduce several additional notational shorthands. By definition the strategy $\strategy$ contains measurement
   175	  operators for each of the possible question types and content
   176	  summarized in \cref{fig:decider_pauli}, such as $\{M^{(\Point,
   177	    W),y}_a\}_{a\in\F_q}$ for all $y\in\F_q^m$, etc. 
   178	For ``line'' questions (of type $\ALine$ or $\DLine$) we will use
   179	 $\Line$ as a formal placeholder for either type $\ALine$ or $\DLine$;
   180	  which type is meant will be clear from the nature of the
   181	  line. Moreover, we will use $\ell$ to denote the description of
   182	  either an axis-parallel line (given by a pair $\ell=(u_0, s)$) or a
   183	  diagonal line (given by a triple $\ell=(u_0, s, v)$). We also introduce the following collection of observables constructed from the
   184	  measurement operators in the strategy. 	
   185		For every $u \in
   186	  \F_q^m$, $r \in \F_q$, and $W \in \{X, Z\}$, define
   187	  \begin{equation}
   188	    W^r(u) =\sum_{a\in\F_q} (-1)^{\tr(ar)}  M^{(\Point, W), u}_a\;. \label{eq:qld-strat-obs}
   189	  \end{equation}

   197	\begin{lemma}
   198	\label{lem:qld-win-implications}
   199	Assume that $\strategy$ succeeds in $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ with probability at least $1-\eps$, for some $\eps\geq 0$. Then the following hold: 
   200		\begin{enumerate}
   201			\item \label{enu:qld-cons} (\textbf{Consistency check}) On average over $(\tvar,x)$ sampled from the question distribution of $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$, we have that $M^{\tvar,x}_a \otimes \Id_\bob \simeq_\eps \Id_\alice \otimes M^{\tvar,x}_a$.
   202			\item \label{enu:qld-ld} (\textbf{Low-degree check})
   203	                  For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, on average over $(\line,u)$
   204	                  drawn from the line-point distribution (see
   205	                  Definition~\ref{def:line-point-dist}), we
   206	                  have $M^{(\Line,W),\line}_{[\eval_u(\cdot) = a]} \otimes \Id_\bob \simeq_\eps \Id_\alice \otimes M^{(\Point,W),u}_a$, where the answer summation is over $a \in \F_q$. 
   207			
   208		\item \label{enu:qld-pauli-basis-cons} (\textbf{Pauli basis consistency check}) For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, on average over $u \in \F_q^m$, we have $M^{(\Point,W),u}_a \otimes \Id_\bob \simeq_\eps \Id_\alice \otimes M^{(\Pauli,W)}_{[g_h(u)=a]}$ where $M^{(\Pauli,W)}_{[g_h(u)=a]} = \sum_{h \in \F_q^{\nqubits} : g_h(u) = a} M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h$ and $g_h$ is the low-degree encoding of $h$. 
   209		
   210			\item \label{enu:qld-comm} (\textbf{Commutation check}) For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, on average over commuting $\omega = (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)$, we have $M^{(\Pair,W),\omega}_a \otimes \Id_\bob \simeq_\eps \Id_\alice \otimes M^{\Pair,\omega}_{[\beta_W = a]}$, where the answer summation is over $a \in \F_2$.
   211			\item \label{enu:qld-comm-cons} (\textbf{Commutation consistency check}) For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, on average over commuting $\omega = (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)$, we have $M^{(\Point,W),u_W}_{[\tr(\cdot r_W) = a]} \otimes \Id_\bob \simeq_\eps \Id_\alice \otimes M^{(\Pair,W),\omega}_{a}$, where the answer summation is over $a\in \F_2$.
   212			
   213			\item\label{enu:qld-ms} (\textbf{Magic square check}) For any anticommuting $\omega = (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)$ let $\Lambda_\omega$ be the value of the strategy $\Big (\ket{\psi}, \{M^{\Constraint_i,\omega}_{\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3}\} \cup \{M^{\Variable_j,\omega}_a \} \Big )$ in the game $\game^\ms$. Then 
   214			\[
   215				\E_{\omega \, : \, \tr((r_\xpt \cdot
   216	                          u_\xpt) \cdot (r_\zpt \cdot u_\zpt)) \neq 0} \Lambda_\omega = 1 - O(\eps)\;.
   217			\]
   218	
   219		\item \label{enu:qld-ms-cons} (\textbf{Magic square consistency check}) For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, on average over anticommuting $\omega = (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)$,
   220		\begin{gather}
   221			M^{(\Point,X),u_\xpt}_{[\tr(\cdot r_\xpt) = a]} \otimes \Id_\bob \simeq_\eps \Id_\alice \otimes M^{\Variable_1,\omega}_{a} \;,\\
   222			M^{(\Point,Z),u_\zpt}_{[\tr(\cdot r_\zpt) = a]} \otimes \Id_\bob \simeq_\eps \Id_\alice \otimes M^{\Variable_5,\omega}_{a}\;,
   223		\end{gather}	
   224		where the answer summations are over $\F_2$.

   200	noncomputable def ldQuestionDistribution (P : LdParams) :

   265	def evalCoefficient {K : Type*} [Semiring K] {n : ℕ}

   278	  | .dline, .dlinePolys _ => true

   281	/-- The axis-parallel line/point relation in `def:ld-win-predicate`, blueprint

   285	def alinePointCondition (P : LdParams) (line point : LdSpace P)
   286	    (f : Fin P.k → Fin (P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P)
   287	    (a : Fin P.k → ScalarQ P) : Prop :=

   291	    point.point = line.point + t • coordinateDirection (chiIndex P line.seed) →

   293	
   294	/-- The diagonal line/point relation in `def:ld-win-predicate`, blueprint
   295	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
   296	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   297	-/
   298	def dlinePointCondition (P : LdParams) (line point : LdSpace P)
   299	    (f : Fin P.k → Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P)
   300	    (a : Fin P.k → ScalarQ P) : Prop :=
   301	  ∀ t : ScalarQ P,
   302	    point.point = line.point + t • line.direction →
   303	      ∀ j : Fin P.k, evalCoefficient (f j) t = a j
   304	
   305	/-- The low-degree consistency predicate, rejecting answers of the wrong
   306	constructor shape.  This is `def:ld-win-predicate` in
   307	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
   308	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   309	-/
   310	noncomputable def ldWinPredicate (P : LdParams) :
   311	    LdQuestion P → LdQuestion P → LdAnswer P → LdAnswer P → Bool :=
   312	  open Classical in
   313	  fun (tA, xA) (tB, xB) a b =>
   314	      if validLdAnswer tA a && validLdAnswer tB b then
   315	        match tA, tB, a, b with
   316	        | .point, .point, .pointVals u, .pointVals v => decide (u = v)
   317	        | .aline, .point, .alinePolys f, .pointVals u =>
   318	            decide (alinePointCondition P xA xB f u)
   319	        | .point, .aline, .pointVals u, .alinePolys f =>
   320	            decide (alinePointCondition P xB xA f u)
   321	        | .dline, .point, .dlinePolys f, .pointVals u =>
   322	            decide (dlinePointCondition P xA xB f u)
   323	        | .point, .dline, .pointVals u, .dlinePolys f =>
   324	            decide (dlinePointCondition P xB xA f u)
   325	        | .aline, .aline, .alinePolys f, .alinePolys g => decide (f = g)
   326	        | .dline, .dline, .dlinePolys f, .dlinePolys g => decide (f = g)
   327	        | _, _, _, _ => true
   328	      else false
   329	
   330	/-- The low-degree game packaged as a `Game`.  This is `def:ld-game` in
   331	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-105`, paper origin
   332	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   333	-/
   334	noncomputable def ldGame (P : LdParams) : Game where
   335	  QuestionA := LdQuestion P
   336	  QuestionB := LdQuestion P
   337	  AnswerA := LdAnswer P
   338	  AnswerB := LdAnswer P
   339	  μ := ldQuestionDistribution P
   340	  μ_prob := by sorry
   341	  decide := ldWinPredicate P
   342	
   343	end
   344	
   345	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

1	\section{Nonlocal Games and $\MIP^*$}
     2	\label{sec:games}
     3	
     4	We introduce definitions associated with nonlocal games and strategies that will
     5	be used throughout.
     6	
     7	\subsection{Games and strategies}
     8	\label{sec:strat}
     9	
    10	\begin{definition}[Two-player one-round games]
    11	  \label{def:game}
    12	  A \emph{two-player one-round game} $\game$ is specified by a tuple
    13	  $(\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ where
    14	  \begin{enumerate}
    15	  \item $\cal{X}$ and $\cal{Y}$ are finite sets (called the \emph{question
    16	      alphabets}),
    17	  \item $\cal{A}$ and $\cal{B}$ are finite sets (called the \emph{answer
    18	      alphabets}),
    19	  \item $\mu$ is a probability distribution over $\cal{X} \times \cal{Y}$
    20	    (called the \emph{question distribution}), and
    21	  \item $D: \cal{X} \times \cal{Y} \times \cal{A} \times \cal{B} \to \{0,1\}$ is
    22	    a function (called the \emph{decision predicate}).
    23	  \end{enumerate}
    24	\end{definition}
    25	
    26	\begin{definition}[Tensor product strategies]
    27	  \label{def:tensor-product-strategy}
    28	  A \emph{tensor product strategy} $\strategy$ for a game $\game = (\cal{X},
    29	  \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ is a tuple $(\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ where
    30	  \begin{itemize}
    31		\item $\ket{\psi}$ is a pure quantum state, i.e.\ a unit vector in $\mH_A \otimes \mH_B$ for finite
    32	    dimensional complex Hilbert spaces $\mH_A, \mH_B$,
    33		\item $A$ is a set $\{A^x\}$ such that for every $x \in \cal{X}$, $A^x =
    34	    \{A^x_a \}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ is a POVM over $\mH_A$, and
    35		\item $B$ is a set $\{B^y\}$ such that for every $y \in \cal{Y}$, $B^y =
    36	    \{B^y_b \}_{b \in \cal{B}}$ is a POVM over $\mH_B$.
    37	\end{itemize}
    38	\end{definition}
    39	
    40	\begin{definition}[Tensor product value]
    41	  \label{def:tensor-product-value}
    42		The \emph{tensor product value} of a tensor product strategy $\strategy =
    43	  (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$  with respect to a game $\game=(\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A},
    44	  \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ is defined as
    45	  \begin{equation*}
    46			\val^*(\game, \strategy) = \sum_{x,\, y,\, a,\, b} \, \mu(x,y)\, D(x,y,a,b)\,
    47	    \bra{\psi} A^x_a \otimes B^y_b\, \ket{\psi}\;.
    48	  \end{equation*}
    49		For $v\in[0,1]$ we say that the strategy $\strategy$ \emph{passes (or wins)
    50	    $\game$ with probability $v$ if} $\val^*(\game, \strategy) \geq v$.
    51	  The \emph{tensor product value} of $\game$ is defined as
    52	  \begin{equation*}
    53			\val^*(\game) = \sup_\strategy \val^*(\game, \strategy)\;,
    54	  \end{equation*}
    55		where the supremum is taken over all tensor product strategies $\strategy$ for
    56	  $\game$.
    57	\end{definition}
    58	
    59	
    60	\begin{remark}
    61	  Unless specified otherwise, all strategies considered in this paper are tensor
    62	  product strategies, and we simply call them \emph{strategies}.
    63	  Similarly, we refer to $\val^*(\game)$ as the \emph{value} of the game
    64	  $\game$.
    65	\end{remark}
    66	
    67	
    68	\begin{definition}[Projective strategies]
    69	  \label{def:projective-strategy}
    70	  We say that a strategy $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ is \emph{projective} if
    71	  all the measurements $\{A^x_a\}_a$ and $\{B^y_b\}_b$ are projective.
    72	\end{definition}
    73	
    74	\begin{definition}\label{rem:symmetric-games}
    75		A game $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ is
    76	  \emph{symmetric} if the question and answer alphabets are the same for both
    77	  players (i.e.\
    78	  $\cal{X} = \cal{Y}$ and $\cal{A} = \cal{B}$), the distribution $\mu$ is
    79	  symmetric (i.e.\
    80	  $\mu(x,y) = \mu(y,x)$), and the decision predicate $D$ treats both players
    81	  symmetrically (i.e.\ for all $x,y,a,b$, $D(x,y,a,b) = D(y,x,b,a)$).
    82	 
    83	We call a strategy $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$
    84	  \emph{symmetric} if $\ket{\psi}$ is a (pure) state in $\mH \otimes \mH$, for some
    85	  Hilbert space $\mH$, that is invariant under permutation of the two factors,
    86	  and the measurement operators of both players are identical.
    87	\end{definition}
    88	
    89	We often specify symmetric games $\game$ and symmetric strategies $\strategy$ using
    90	  a compact notation: we write $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{A}, \mu, D)$ and
    91	  $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, M)$ where $M$ denotes the set of measurement
    92	  operators for both players.
    93	
    94	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:symmetric-strat}
    95	  Let $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{A},  \mu, D)$ be a symmetric game
    96	  such that $\val^*(\game) = 1-\eps$ for some $\eps\geq 0$.
    97	  Then there exists a symmetric and projective strategy
    98	  $\strategy=(\ket{\psi},M)$ such that $\val^*(\game,\strategy)\geq 1-\eps$.
    99	\end{lemma}
   100	
   101	\begin{proof}
   102	  By definition for any $\eps'>\eps$ there exists a strategy $\strategy'= (\ket{\psi'},A,B)$ such
   103	  that $\val^*(\game,\strategy')\geq 1-\eps'$.
   104	Using Naimark's theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:naimark}) we can assume
   105	without loss of generality that $\ket{\psi'}\in\C_{\alice'}^d\otimes \C_{\bob'}^d$ for some integer $d$
   106	  and that for every $x$, $A^x$ and $B^x$ are projective measurements.
   107	Let
   108	  \[
   109	    \ket{\psi} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \big( \ket{0}_\alice \ket{1}_\bob
   110	    \ket{\psi'}_{\alice'\bob'} + \ket{1}_\alice \ket{0}_\bob
   111	    \ket{\psi'_\tau}_{\alice'\bob'}\big) \in (\C_{\alice}^2 \otimes
   112	    \C_{\alice'}^d) \otimes (\C_\bob^2 \otimes \C_{\bob'}^d)\;,
   113	  \]
   114	  where $\ket{\psi'_\tau}$ is obtained from $\ket{\psi}$ by permuting the two
   115	  players' registers.
   116	  Observe that $\ket{\psi}$ is invariant under permutation of $\alice\alice'$
   117	  and $\bob\bob'$.
   118	
   119	  For any question $x\in \cal{X}$ define the measurement $M^x = \{M^x_a\}_{a \in \cal{A}}$
   120	  acting on the Hilbert space $\C^2 \otimes \C^d$ as follows:
   121	  \[
   122	  	M^x_a = \ketbra{0}{0} \otimes A^x_a + \ketbra{1}{1} \otimes B^x_a \;,
   123	  \]
   124		i.e.\ for $\ket{\varphi} \in \C^d$, $M^x_a(\ket{0}\ket{\varphi})=\ket{0}A^x_a\ket{\varphi}$ and $M^x_a(\ket{1}\ket{\varphi})=\ket{1}B^x_a\ket{\varphi}$.
   125	  When Alice receives question $x$, she measures $M^x$ on registers $\alice \alice'$, and when Bob receives 
   126	  question $y$, he measures $M^y$ on registers $\bob \bob'$.
   127	Using that by assumption the decision predicate $D$ for $\game$ is symmetric,
   128	  it is not hard to verify that $\val^*(\game,\strategy) =
   129	  \val^*(\game,\strategy')$.
   130	\end{proof}

   132	\begin{definition}
   133	  \label{def:comm-strategy}
   134	  Let $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ be a game, and let
   135	  $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ be a strategy for $\game$ such that  $\mH_A = \mH_B$.
   136	  Let $S \subseteq \cal{X} \times \cal{Y}$ denote the support of the question
   137	  distribution $\mu$, i.e.\ the set of $(x,y)$ such that $\mu(x,y)>0$.
   138	  We say that $\strategy$ is a \emph{commuting strategy for $\game$} if for all
   139	  question pairs $(x, y) \in S$, we have $[A^x_a, B^y_b] = 0$ 
   140	  for all $a
   141	  \in \cal{A}, b \in \cal{B}$, where $[A, B] = AB - BA$ denotes the commutator.
   142	\end{definition}
   143	
   144	\begin{definition}[Consistent measurements]
   145	  \label{def:consistent-measurement}
   146	  Let $\cal{A}$ be a finite set, let $\ket{\psi} \in \mH \otimes \mH$ be a
   147	  state, and let $\{ M_a \}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ be a projective measurement on
   148	  $\mH$.
   149	  We say that \emph{$\{M_a\}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$} if
   150	  and only if
   151	  \begin{equation*}
   152	    \forall a \in \mA\;,\quad M_a \otimes \Id_\bob\, \ket{\psi}
   153	    = \Id_\alice \otimes M_a\, \ket{\psi}\;.
   154	  \end{equation*}
   155		When the state $\ket{\psi}$ is clear from context we simply say that \emph{$\{M_a\}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ is consistent}.
   156	\end{definition}
   157	
   158	The terminology ``consistent'' arises from the fact that when the measurement $\{M_a\}$ is performed on both registers of $\ket{\psi}$, the probability of obtaining twice the same outcome is 
   159	\[ \sum_a \bra{\psi} M_a \otimes M_a \ket{\psi}\,=\, \sum_a \bra{\psi} \Id_\alice \otimes (M_a)^2 \ket{\psi} \,=\, \sum_a \bra{\psi} \Id_\alice \otimes M_a \ket{\psi} \,=\,1\;,\]
   160	where the first equality is by definition of consistency, the second uses that $\{M_a\}$ is projective, and the last uses $\sum_a M_a=\Id$. 
   161	
   162	\begin{definition}[Consistent strategies]
   163	  \label{def:consistent-strategy}
   164		Let $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ be a projective strategy with state
   165	  $\ket{\psi} \in \mH \otimes \mH$, for some Hilbert space~$\mH$, which is
   166	  defined on question alphabets $\cal{X}$ and~$\cal{Y}$ and answer alphabets
   167	  $\cal{A}$ and~$\cal{B}$, respectively.
   168	  We say that the strategy $\strategy$ is \emph{consistent} if for all $x \in
   169	  \cal{X}$, the measurement $\{A^x_a\}_{a \in \cal{A}}$ is consistent on
   170	  $\ket{\psi}$ and if for all $y \in \cal{Y}$, the measurement $\{B^y_b\}_{b \in
   171	    \cal{B}}$ is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$.
   172	\end{definition}
   173	
   174	We almost always restrict our attention to symmetric strategies. In this case, consistency implies that whenever both players are sent the same question, they provide the same answer. 
   175	
   176	\begin{definition}
   177	  \label{def:spcc}
   178	  We say that a strategy $\strategy$ for a game $\game$ is \emph{PCC} if it is projective, consistent, and commuting for $\game$.
   179	  Additionally, we say that a PCC strategy $\strategy$ is \emph{SPCC} if it is furthermore symmetric.
   180	\end{definition}
   181	
   182	
   183	Recall that for a (pure) state $\ket{\psi}\in \mH_\alice \otimes \mH_\bob$, the \emph{Schmidt rank} of $\ket{\psi}$ is the smallest integer $k$ such that 
   184	\[ \ket{\psi} = \sum_{i=1}^k\, \alpha_i \ket{u_i}\otimes \ket{v_i}\;,\]
   185	for some orthonormal families $\{\ket{u_i}\}\subset \mH_\alice$ and $\{\ket{v_i}\}\subset\mH_\bob$ and $\alpha_i>0$. The coefficients $\alpha_i$ are uniquely defined by $\ket{\psi}$ and called \emph{Schmidt coefficients}. The state $\ket{\psi}$ is called \emph{maximally entangled} if $\alpha_i=\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}$ for all $i=1,\ldots,k$.  
   186	
   187	
   188	\begin{definition}[Entanglement requirements of a game]
   189	  \label{def:ent}
   190		For all games $\game$ and $\nu \in [0, 1]$, let $\Ent(\game, \nu)$ denote the
   191	  minimum integer $d$ such that there exists a finite dimensional tensor product
   192	  strategy $\strategy$ that achieves success probability at least $\nu$ in the
   193	  game $\game$ with a state $\ket{\psi}$ whose Schmidt rank is at most $d$.
   194	  If there is no finite dimensional strategy that achieves success probability
   195	  $\nu$, then define $\Ent(\game, \nu)$ to be $\infty$.
   196	\end{definition}
   197	
   198

   200	\begin{remark}
   201	  A strategy $\strategy = (\ket{\psi},A,B)$ for a symmetric game $\game =
   202	  (\cal{X}, \cal{X}, \cal{A}, \cal{A}, \mu, D)$ is called \emph{synchronous} if
   203	  it holds that for every $x\in \cal{X}$ and $a\neq b \in \cal{A}$, $\bra{\psi}
   204	  A^x_a \otimes B^x_b \ket{\psi} = 0$; in other words,
   205	  the players never return different answers when simultaneously asked the same
   206	  question.
   207	  As shown in~\cite{paulsen2016estimating} the condition for a
   208	  finite-dimensional strategy of being synchronous is equivalent to the
   209	  condition that it is projective, consistent, and moreover $\ket{\psi}$ is a
   210	  maximally entangled state.
   211	  (The equivalence is extended to infinite-dimensional strategies, as well as
   212	  correlations induced by limits of finite-dimensional strategies,
   213	  in~\cite{kim2018synchronous}.)
   214	\end{remark}
   215	\subsection{Distance measures}
   216	
   217	We introduce several distance measures that are used throughout.
   218	
   219	\begin{definition}[Distance between states]
   220	  \label{def:state-distance}
   221	
   222		Let $\{\ket{\psi_n}\}_{n\in \N}$ and $\{\ket{\psi'_n}\}_{n\in \N}$ be two
   223	  families of states in the same space $\mH$.
   224	  For some function $\delta : \N \to [0,1]$ we say that $\{ \ket{\psi_n} \}$ and
   225	  $\{ \ket{\psi'_n} \}$ are \emph{$\delta$-close}, denoted as $\ket{\psi}
   226	  \approx_\delta \ket{\psi'}$, if $ \norm{\ket{\psi_n} - \ket{\psi'_n}}^2 =
   227	  O(\delta(n))$.
   228	  (For convenience we generally leave the dependence of the states and $\delta$
   229	  on the indexing parameter $n$ implicit, writing e.g.\ $\ket{\psi}$ for $\ket{\psi_n}$.)
   230	\end{definition}
   231	
   232	\begin{definition}[Consistency between POVMs]
   233	  \label{def:consistency}
   234		Let $\mX$ be a finite set and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mX$.
   235	  Let $\ket{\psi} \in \cal{H}_A \otimes \cal{H}_B$ be a quantum state, and for
   236	  all $x\in \mX$, $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ POVMs.
   237	  We write
   238	  \begin{equation*}
   239	    A^x_a \otimes I_\bob \simeq_\delta I_\alice \otimes B^x_a
   240	  \end{equation*}
   241	  on state $\ket{\psi}$ and distribution $\mu$ if
   242	  \begin{equation*}
   243	    \E_{x\sim \mu} \sum_{a\ne b} \bra{\psi} A^x_a \otimes B^x_b \ket{\psi}
   244	    = O(\delta)\;.\footnote{Here the use of the $O(\cdot)$ notation refers to the fact that the notation will often be used to measure consistency for \emph{famillies} of POVM and states indexed by an implicit parameter $n\in \mathbb{N}$, which will always be clear from context but omitted for legibility, see Definition~\ref{def:state-distance}. The $O(\cdot)$ is taken as $n\to\infty$.}
   245	  \end{equation*}
   246	  In this case, we say that $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ are
   247	  \emph{$\delta$-consistent} on $\ket{\psi}$.
   248	\end{definition}
   249	
   250	Note that a consistent measurement on $\ket{\psi}$ according to
   251	Definition~\ref{def:consistent-measurement} is $0$-consistent with itself on the same $\ket{\psi}$ and under
   252	the singleton distribution, according to Definition~\ref{def:consistency} (and
   253	vice-versa). This is because 
   254	\[ \sum_a \bra{\psi} M_a \otimes M_a \ket{\psi} =1 \,\implies \, \forall a\;,\;\Id\otimes M_a \ket{\psi} = M_a \otimes \Id \ket{\psi}\;,\]
   255	because using that $\{M_a\}$ is a POVM there must be equality in the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality
   256	\[ 1 = \sum_a \bra{\psi} M_a \otimes M_a \ket{\psi}\, \leq\, \Big(\sum_a \|\Id\otimes M_a \ket{\psi}\|^2 \Big)\Big(\sum_a \|M_a\otimes \Id \ket{\psi}\|^2 \Big)^{1/2} \,\leq\,1 \;.\]
   257	
   258	\begin{definition}[Distance between POVMs]
   259	  \label{def:povm-distance}
   260		Let $\mX$ be a finite set and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mX$. 
   261	  Let $\ket{\psi} \in \cal{H}$ be a quantum state, and for all $x\in \mX$,
   262	  $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{N^x_a\}$ two POVMs on $\mH$.
   263	  We say that \emph{$\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{N^x_a\}$ are $\delta$-close on state
   264	    $\ket{\psi}$ and under distribution $\mu$} if
   265	  \begin{equation*}
   266	    \E_{x\sim \mu} \sum_a \norm{ (M^x_a - N^x_a) \ket{\psi} }^2 \leq O(\delta)\;,
   267	  \end{equation*}
   268	  and we write $M^x_a \approx_\delta N^x_a$ to denote this when the state
   269	  $\ket{\psi}$ and distribution $\mu$ are clear from context.
   270	  This distance is referred to as the \emph{state-dependent} distance.
   271	\end{definition}
   272	
   273	\begin{definition}[Distance between strategies]
   274	  \label{def:strategy-distance}
   275	  Let $\game = (\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$ be a nonlocal game
   276	  and let $\strategy = (\psi, A, B)$, $\strategy' = (\psi', A', B')$ be 
   277	  strategies for $\game$.
   278	  For $\delta\in[0,1]$ we say that \emph{$\strategy$ is $\delta$-close to
   279	    $\strategy'$} if the following conditions hold.
   280	  \begin{enumerate}
   281		\item The states $\ket{\psi}, \ket{\psi'}$ are states in the same
   282	    Hilbert space $\mH_A \otimes \mH_B$ and are $\delta$-close.
   283		\item For all $x \in \cal{X}, y \in \cal{Y}$, we have $A^x_a \approx_\delta
   284	    (A')^x_a$ and $B^y_b \approx_\delta (B')^y_b$, with the approximations
   285	    holding under the distribution $\mu$, and on either $\ket{\psi}$ or
   286	    $\ket{\psi'}$.
   287	  \end{enumerate}
   288	\end{definition}
   289	
   290	We record several useful facts about the consistency measure and the
   291	state-dependent distance without proof.
   292	Readers are referred to Sections 4.4 and 4.5 in~\cite{NW19} for additional
   293	discussion and proofs.
   294	
   295	\begin{fact}[Fact 4.13 and Fact 4.14 in~\cite{NW19}]
   296	  \label{fact:agreement}
   297	  For POVMs $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$, the following hold.
   298	  \begin{enumerate}
   299	  \item If $A^x_a \otimes I_\bob \simeq_\delta I_\alice \otimes B^x_a$ then
   300	    $A^x_a \otimes I_\bob \approx_\delta I_\alice \otimes B^x_a$.
   301	    \label{item:consistency-implies-approx}
   302	  \item If $A^x_a \otimes I_\bob \approx_\delta I_\alice \otimes B^x_a$
   303	    \emph{and} $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ are projective measurements, then
   304	    $A^x_a \otimes I_\bob \simeq_\delta I_\alice \otimes B^x_a$.
   305	    \label{item:both-projectors-implies-consistency}
   306	  \item If $A^x_a \otimes I_\bob \approx_\delta I_\alice \otimes B^x_a$ and
   307	    either $\{A^x_a\}$ or $\{B^x_a\}$ is a projective measurement, then
   308	    $A^x_a \otimes I_\bob \simeq_{\delta^{1/2}} I_\alice \otimes B^x_a$.
   309	    \label{item:one-projector-implies-consistency}
   310	  \end{enumerate}
   311	\end{fact}
   312	
   313	\begin{fact}[Fact 4.20 in~\cite{NW19}]
   314	  \label{fact:add-a-proj}
   315	  Let $\cal{A},\cal{B},\cal{C}$ be finite sets, and let $\mu$ be a distribution
   316	  over question pairs $(x,y)$.
   317	  Let $\{A_{a,b}^x\}$ and $\{B_{a,b}^x\}$ be operators whose outcomes range over the
   318	  product set $\cal{A} \times \cal{B}$.
   319	  Suppose a set of operators $\{C_{a,c}^y\}$, whose outcomes range over the
   320	  product set $\cal{A} \times \cal{C}$, satisfies the condition $\sum_{c}
   321	  (C_{a,c}^y)^\dagger C_{a,c}^y \leq \Id$ for all $a$ and all $y$.
   322	  If $A_{a,b}^x \approx_\delta B_{a,b}^x$ on average over $x$ sampled from the
   323	  corresponding marginal of distribution $\mu$, then $C^y_{a,c} A^x_{a,b}
   324	  \approx_\delta C^y_{a,c} B^x_{a,b}$ on average over $(x,y)$ sampled from $\mu$.
   325	\end{fact}
   326	\begin{proof}
   327	  Fix questions $x,y$ and answers $a \in \cal{A},b \in \cal{B}$. We have then that
   328	  \begin{align}
   329	    \sum_{c} \left \| (C^y_{a,c} A^x_{a,b} - C^y_{a,c} B^x_{a,b} ) \ket{\psi} \right \|^2
   330	    & = \sum_{c} \bra{\psi} (A^x_{a,b} - B^x_{a,b})^\dagger (C^y_{a,c})^\dagger (C^y_{a,c})
   331	      (A^x_{a,b} - B^x_{a,b} ) \ket{\psi}\\
   332	    & \leq \bra{\psi} (A^x_{a,b} - B^x_{a,b})^\dagger
   333	      (A^x_{a,b} - B^x_{a,b} ) \ket{\psi} \\
   334	    & = \left \| (A^x_{a,b} - B^x_{a,b})\ket{\psi} \right \|^2
   335	  \end{align}
   336	  where the inequality follows from the assumption that $\sum_c (C_{a,c}^y)^\dagger
   337	  C_{a,c}^y \leq \Id$.
   338	  Thus we obtain the desired conclusion
   339	  \begin{equation*}
   340	    \E_{(x,y) \sim \mu} \sum_{a,b,c} \left \| (C^y_{a,c} A^x_{a,b} - C^y_{a,c} B^x_{a,b} )
   341	      \ket{\psi} \right \|^2 	\leq \E_{(x,y) \sim \mu} \sum_{a,b}
   342	    \left \| (A^x_{a,b} - B^x_{a,b})\ket{\psi} \right \|^2 \leq \delta.
   343	  \end{equation*}
   344	\end{proof}

   346	
   347	\begin{fact}
   348	\label{fact:add-a-proj2}
   349	Let $\mathcal{X},\mathcal{A}$ denote finite sets, and let $\mathcal{G}$ denote a set of functions $g: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{A}$. Let $\{A^x_a \}$, $\{B^x_a\}$ be POVMs indexed by $\mathcal{X}$ and outcomes in $\mathcal{A}$. Let $\{ S_g^x \}_{x\in \mathcal{X}, g\in\mathcal{G}}$ denote a set of operators such that for all $x \in \mathcal{X}$, $\sum_g (S_g^x)^\dagger S_g^x \leq \Id$. 
   350	If $A^x_a \approx_\delta B^x_a$ on average over $x$, then $S_g^x A^x_{g(x)} \approx_\delta S_g^x B^x_{g(x)}$. 
   351	\end{fact}
   352	\begin{proof}
   353		We expand:
   354		\begin{align*}
   355			\E_x \sum_g \norm{ S^x_g (A^x_{g(x)} - B^x_{g(x)}) \ket{\psi}}^2 &= \E_x \sum_g \bra{\psi} (A^x_{g(x)} - B^x_{g(x)})^\dagger  (S_g^x)^\dagger S_g^x (A^x_{g(x)} - B^x_{g(x)}) \ket{\psi} \\
   356			&= \E_x \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A^x_a - B^x_a)^\dagger  \Big(\sum_{g: g(x) = a} (S_g^x)^\dagger S_g^x \Big) (A^x_a - B^x_a) \ket{\psi} \\
   357			&\leq \E_x \sum_a \bra{\psi} (A^x_a - B^x_a)^\dagger (A^x_a - B^x_a) \ket{\psi} \\
   358			&= \E_x \sum_a \norm{ (A^x_a - B^x_a) \ket{\psi} }^2.
   359		\end{align*}
   360		The inequality follows from the fact that $\sum_{g: g(x) = a} (S_g^x)^\dagger S_g^x \leq \sum_g (S_g^x)^\dagger (S_g^x) \leq \Id$. The last line is at most $\delta$ by assumption, and we obtain the desired conclusion.
   361	\end{proof}

   404	The state-dependent distance is the right tool for reasoning about the closeness
   405	of measurement operators in a strategy.
   406	The following lemma ensures that, when two families of measurements are close on a
   407	state, changing from one family of measurement to the other only introduces
   408	a small error to the value of the strategy.
   409	
   410	\begin{lemma}
   411	  \label{lem:commutation-analysis}
   412	  Let $\{A^x_{a,\, b}\}$, $\{B^x_{a,\, b,\, c}\}$, $\{C^x_{a,\, c}\}$ be POVMs.
   413	  Suppose $\{B^x_{a,\, b,\, c}\}$ is projective, and
   414	  \begin{align*}
   415	    A^x_{a,\, b} \otimes \Id_\bob &\approx_\delta \Id_\alice \otimes B^x_{a,\, b}\;,\\
   416	    C^x_{a,\, c} \otimes \Id_\bob &\approx_\delta \Id_\alice \otimes B^x_{a,\, c}\;,
   417	  \end{align*}
   418		where recall that $B^x_{a,\, b} = \sum_c B^x_{a,b,c}$ and similarly $B^x_{a,\, c}=\sum_b B^x_{a,b,c}$. 
   419	  Then the following approximate commutation relation holds:
   420	  \begin{equation*}
   421	    [A^x_{a,\, b}, C^x_{a,\, c}] \otimes I_\bob \approx_\delta 0\;.
   422	  \end{equation*}
   423	\end{lemma}
   424	
   425	\begin{proof}
   426	  Applying Fact~\ref{fact:add-a-proj} to $C^x_{a,\, c} \otimes \Id_\bob
   427	  \approx_\delta \Id_\alice \otimes B^x_{a,\, c}$ and $\{A^x_{a,b} \otimes
   428	  \Id_\bob \}$, we have
   429	  \begin{equation}
   430	    \label{eq:commutation-analysis-1}
   431	    A^x_{a,\, b} C^x_{a,\, c} \otimes \Id_\bob
   432	    \approx_\delta A^x_{a,\, b} \otimes B^x_{a,\, c}\,.
   433	  \end{equation}
   434	  Similarly, applying Fact~\ref{fact:add-a-proj} to $A^x_{a,\, b} \otimes
   435	  \Id_\bob \approx_\delta \Id_\alice \otimes B^x_{a,\, b}$ and $\{\Id_\alice
   436	  \otimes B^x_{a,c}\}$, and using the fact that $\{B^x_{a,b,c}\}$ is projective,
   437	  we have
   438	  \begin{equation}
   439	    \label{eq:commutation-analysis-2}
   440	    \begin{split}
   441	      A^x_{a,\, b} \otimes B^x_{a,\, c}
   442	      & \approx_\delta \Id_\alice \otimes B^x_{a,\, c} B^x_{a,\, b}\\
   443	      & =_{\phantom{\delta}} \Id_\alice \otimes B^x_{a,\, b,\, c}\,.
   444	    \end{split}
   445	  \end{equation}
   446	  Combining Equations~\eqref{eq:commutation-analysis-1}
   447	  and~\eqref{eq:commutation-analysis-2}, we have
   448	  \begin{equation}
   449	    \label{eq:commutation-analysis-3}
   450	    A^x_{a,\, b} C^x_{a,\, c} \otimes \Id_\bob \approx_\delta
   451	    \Id_\alice \otimes B^x_{a,\, b,\, c}\,.
   452	  \end{equation}
   453	  A similar argument gives
   454	  \begin{equation}
   455	    \label{eq:commutation-analysis-4}
   456	    C^x_{a,\, c} A^x_{a,\, b} \otimes \Id_\bob \approx_\delta
   457	    \Id_\alice \otimes B^x_{a,\, b,\, c}\,.
   458	  \end{equation}
   459	  The claim follows from Equations~\eqref{eq:commutation-analysis-3}
   460	  and~\eqref{eq:commutation-analysis-4}.
   461	\end{proof}

   466	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:ld-sandwich}
   467	  Let $k \geq 0$ be an integer and let $\eps>0$.
   468	  Let $\mX$ be a finite set and $\mu$ a distribution over $\mX$.
   469	  For each $1 \leq i \leq k$ let $\mG_i$ be a finite set of functions $g_i : \mY
   470	  \rightarrow \mR_i$ and for each $x \in \mX$ let $\{G^{i,\, x}_g\}_{g\in
   471	    \mG_i}$ be a projective measurement.

   473	  property: for any two $g_i \neq g_i' \in \mG_i$, the probability that $g_i(y)
   474	  = g_i'(y)$ over a uniformly random $y \in \mY$ is at most $\eps$.
   475	
   476	  Let $\bigl\{ A^{x}_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots\,,\, g_k} \bigr\}$ be a projective
   477	  measurement with outcomes $(g_1,\ldots,g_k) \in \mG_1\times\cdots\times
   478	  \mG_k$.

   480	  $y\in \mY$ sampled uniformly at random,
   481	  \begin{equation}\label{eq:ld-sandwich-1}
   482	    A^{x}_{[\eval_y(\cdot)_i = a_i]} \abc G^{i,\, x}_{[\eval_y(\cdot)=a_i]}\;.

   487	    G^{2,\, x}_{g_{k-1}} \, G^{1,\, x}_{g_k} \, G^{2,\, x}_{g_{k-1}} \cdots

   541	\subsection{The class $\MIP^*$}
   542	
   543	The complexity class $\MIP^*$ of \emph{multi-prover interactive proof
   544	  systems with entangled provers} is the class of languages that can be
   545	decided by a \emph{proof system} in which a polynomial-time classical
   546	\emph{verifier} interacts with noncommunicating, computationally unbounded
   547	 \emph{provers} who may share a \emph{finite-dimensional} entangled state. In general there may be polynomially many provers,
   548	and the verifier may interact with them over polynomially many
   549	rounds. In each round, the verifier generates a question for
   550	each prover and receives a response from them. At the end of
   551	the interaction the verifier 
   552	decides to either accept or reject. A language $L$ is in $\MIP^*$ if for
   553	every input $z \in L$, there exists a strategy that the provers can
   554	use to convince the verifier to accept with high probability ($\geq 2/3$), and for every input $z \not\in L$, there is
   555	\emph{no} strategy that the provers can use to convince the verifier
   556	to accept with more than low probability ($\geq 1/3$). The former
   557	property is called \emph{completeness} of the proof system, and the
   558	latter \emph{soundness}. The
   559	completeness and soundness probabilities $2/3$ and $1/3$ may be
   560	amplified by sequentially repeating the protocol. 
   561	
   562	For a formal definition of the class $\MIP^*$, see e.g.~\cite[Section
   563	  6.1]{vidick2016quantum}. 
   564	The main result of this paper is a lower bound, and for this purpose,
   565	it suffices  to restrict our attention to proof
   566	systems which involve only two provers, one round of interaction, and
   567	completeness probability $1$. This class is often denoted $\MIP^*_{1,1/2}(2,1)$. A formal definition for this restricted setting follows. 
   568	
   569	\begin{definition}\label{def:mipstar}
   570	  A language $L$ is in $\MIP^*_{1,1/2}$ if and only if there exist two randomized Turing machines
   571	  $\sampler$ and $\decider$ with the following properties.
   572	  \begin{enumerate}
   573	    \item \textbf{Efficiency:} For every $z\in\{0,1\}^*$ there is
   574	      a game $\game_z = (\cal{X}, \cal{Y}, \cal{A}, \cal{B}, \mu, D)$
   575	      such that:
   576	      \begin{enumerate}
   577	      \item The Turing machine $\sampler$ given input $z$ runs in time $\poly(|z|)$ and returns a
   578	      pair $(x,y) \in \cal{X} \times \cal{Y}$ such that the distribution of $(x,y)$, over the random choices of $\sampler$, is $\mu$.
   579	    \item The Turing machine $\decider$ given as input $z$ and a tuple $(x,y,a,b)
   580	      \in \cal{X} \times \cal{Y} \times \cal{A} \times \cal{B}$ runs in time $\poly(|z|)$ and returns $D(x,y,a,b)$.\footnote{Note that the running time of $\decider$ should be $\poly(|z|)$, even for long inputs $a,b$. This can be ensured by having $D$ return $0$ whenever $x,y,a,b$ are too long with respect to $|z|$.}
   581	    \end{enumerate}
   582	  \item \textbf{Completeness:} If $z \in L$, then $\val^*(\game_z) = 1$
   583	  \item \textbf{Soundness:} If $z \not\in L$, then $\val^*(\game_z) \leq 1/2$.
   584	  \end{enumerate}
   585	  We say that the pair $(\sampler, \decider)$ form an $\MIP^*$
   586	  \emph{verifier} for the language $L$, and the associated family of
   587	  games $\game_z$ are an $\MIP^*$ protocol for $L$.
   588	\end{definition}
   589	
   590	  It is clear that $\MIP^*_{1,1/2}(2,1) \subseteq \MIP^*$ (the
   591	  probability $1/2$ of acceptance of inputs not in the language may be
   592	  reduced to $1/3$ by sequential repetition as noted above). The main result of this paper is that $\RE
   593	  \subseteq \MIP^*_{1,1/2}(2,1)$. Since it is known that $\MIP*\subseteq \RE$ it follows
   594	  that $\MIP^*_{1,1/2}(2,1) = \MIP^* = \RE$. 
   595	
   596	 To show our lower bound it will suffice to consider an even more restricted class of $\MIP^*$
   597	  verifiers, for which the Turing machines $\sampler$ and
   598	  $\decider$ have a special structure which we refer to as
   599	  \emph{normal form}. This is defined in the following subsection.
   600		
   601	\subsection{Normal form verifiers}
   602	\label{sec:normal-form}
   603	
   604	We introduce a normal form for verifiers in nonlocal games.
   605	The normal form uses Turing machines to specify the two actions performed by the
   606	verifier in a game: the generation of questions and the verification of answers.
   607	For the generation of questions, we use the formalism of samplers introduced in
   608	Section~\ref{sec:cls}.
   609	The normal form for verifiers gives a uniform method to specify an infinite
   610	family of nonlocal games.
   611	
   612	\begin{definition}[Decider]
   613	  \label{def:decider}
   614	  A \emph{decider} is a $5$-input Turing machine $\decider$ that on all inputs
   615	  of the form $(n,x,y,a,b)$ where $n$ is an integer and $x,y,a,b \in \{0,1\}^*$,
   616	  $\decider$ halts and returns a single bit.
   617	  Let $\TIME_\decider(n)$ denote the maximum time complexity of $\decider$ over
   618	  all inputs of the form $(n,x,y,a,b)$.
   619		When the decider $\decider$ outputs $0$ we say that it \emph{rejects},
   620	  otherwise we say that it \emph{accepts}.
   621	  Furthermore, we call the input $n$ to a decider the \emph{index}.
   622	\end{definition}
   623	
   624	\begin{definition}
   625	  \label{def:normal-ver}
   626	  A \emph{normal form verifier} is a pair $\verifier = (\sampler, \decider)$
   627	  where $\sampler$ is a sampler with field size $q(n) = 2$ and $\decider$ is a
   628	  decider.
   629	  The description length of $\verifier$ is defined to be $\abs{\verifier} =
   630	  \max \{ \abs{\sampler} ,  \abs{\decider} \}$, the maximum of the description lengths of
   631	  $\sampler$ and $\decider$.
   632	  The number of levels of verifier $\verifier$ is defined to be the number of
   633	  levels of its sampler $\sampler$.
   634	\end{definition}
   635	
   636	Next we introduce a notion of \emph{bounded normal form
   637	  verifiers}, in which a single parameter (in this case, an integer $\lambda$)
   638	specifies a bound on the time complexity of $\verifier$, as well as on the
   639	description length of the verifier.
   640	
   641	\begin{definition}[$\lambda$-bounded verifiers]
   642	  \label{def:lambda}
   643	  Let $\lambda \in \N$ be an integer.
   644	  A normal form verifier $\verifier = (\sampler, \decider)$ is
   645	  \emph{$\lambda$-bounded} if the following two conditions hold
   646	  \begin{enumerate}
   647	  \item The time complexity bounds of the verifier $\TIME_\sampler(n)$,
   648	    $\TIME_\decider(n)$ are at most $n^\lambda$ for $n \ge 2$.\footnote{We do
   649	      not require the bound to hold for $n=1$ as $n^\lambda$ is always $1$ and
   650	      hence it is usually not satisfied.
   651	    }
   652	  \item The description length of the verifier $\abs{\verifier}$ is bounded by $\lambda$.
   653	  \end{enumerate}
   654	\end{definition}
   655	
   656	
   657	Normal form verifiers specify an infinite family of nonlocal games indexed by
   658	natural numbers in the following way.
   659	
   660	\begin{definition}
   661	  \label{def:normal-game}
   662	  Let $\verifier = (\sampler, \decider)$ be a normal form verifier.
   663	  For $n \in \N$, we define the following nonlocal game $\verifier_{n}$ to be
   664	  the \emph{$n$-th game corresponding to the verifier $\verifier$}.
   665	  The question sets $\cal{X}$ and $\cal{Y}$ are $\{0,1\}^{\TIME_\sampler(n)}$.
   666	  The answer sets $\cal{A}$ and $\cal{B}$ are $\{0,1\}^{\TIME_\decider(n)}$.
   667	  The question distribution is the distribution $\mu_{\sampler,\, n}$ specified
   668	  in Definition~\ref{def:sampler-sample}.
   669	  The decision predicate is the function computed by
   670	  $\decider(n,\cdot,\cdot,\cdot,\cdot)$, when the last four inputs are
   671	  restricted to $\cal{X}\times \cal{Y}\times\cal{A}\times\cal{B}$.
   672	  The value of the game is denoted by $\val^*(\verifier_{n})$.
   673	\end{definition}
   674	
   675	We note that the game $\verifier_n$ is well-defined since for a normal form
   676	verifier the distribution $\mu_{\sampler,\, n}$ is supported on
   677	$\{0,1\}^{\TIME_\sampler(n)}\times \{0,1\}^{\TIME_\sampler(n)}$ and a normal
   678	form decider always halts with a single-bit output.
   679	
   680	\begin{definition}[Verifier with commuting strategy]
   681	  \label{def:comm-with-checker}
   682	  Let $\verifier = (\sampler, \decider)$ be a normal form verifier.
   683	  For $v:\N\to [0,1]$ say that $\verifier$ has a \emph{value-$v$ commuting
   684	    strategy} if for all $n \in \N$, the game $\verifier_n$ has a value-$v(n)$
   685	  commuting strategy.
   686	\end{definition}

@@ -0,0 +1,48 @@
+import MIPStarRE.QPBT.Algebra.LowDegreeCode
+
+/-! # Decoding maps for the low-degree code
+
+This file supplies `def:decoding-map` and the Boolean cube embedding from
+`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:445-455`, paper
+`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:917-924`.
+-/
+
+open scoped BigOperators
+
+namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
+
+open MIPStarRE.LDT MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries
+
+/-- The formalization-only embedding of Boolean coordinates into a field used by
+`def:decoding-map`; blueprint `ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:445-455`, paper
+`04_preliminaries.tex:917-924`. -/
+def boolToScalar {K : Type*} [Field K] : Bool → K
+  | false => 0
+  | true => 1
+
+/-- The coordinatewise Boolean-cube embedding used by
+`def:decoding-map`; blueprint `ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:445-455`, paper
+`04_preliminaries.tex:917-924`. -/
+def cubeEmbed {K : Type*} [Field K] {m : ℕ} : Cube m → (Fin m → K) :=
+  fun y i => boolToScalar (y i)
+
+/-- The decoding map `def:decoding-map`, blueprint
+`ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:445-455`, paper `04_preliminaries.tex:917-924`. -/
+noncomputable def decodeAt {K : Type*} [Field K] [DecidableEq K] {m : ℕ}
+    (H : Finset K) (g : (Fin m → K) → K) : Cube m → K :=
+  fun y => if g (cubeEmbed y) ∈ H then g (cubeEmbed y) else 0
+
+/-- Boolean specialization of `def:decoding-map`, blueprint
+`ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:445-455`, paper `04_preliminaries.tex:917-924`. -/
+noncomputable abbrev decodeBool {K : Type*} [Field K] [DecidableEq K] {m : ℕ}
+    (g : (Fin m → K) → K) : Cube m → K :=
+  decodeAt ({0, 1} : Finset K) g
+
+/-- The restricted decoding identity in `def:decoding-map`, blueprint
+`ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:445-455`, paper `04_preliminaries.tex:917-924`. -/
+theorem decodeAt_lowDegreeEnc {K : Type*} [Field K] [DecidableEq K] {m : ℕ}
+    (H : Finset K) (a : Cube m → K) (ha : ∀ y, a y ∈ H) :
+    decodeAt H (lowDegreeEnc a) = a := by
+  sorry
+
+end MIPStarRE.QPBT
diff --git a/MIPStarRE/QPBT/Algebra/PauliTheorems.lean b/MIPStarRE/QPBT/Algebra/PauliTheorems.lean
