   728	  Because~$\cal{O}_A$ and~$\cal{O}_B$ anti-commute,
   729	  \begin{equation}\label{eq:am-i-hermitian}
   730	  \cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X
   731	  = - \cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^X \sigma^Z
   732	  = \cal{O}_B \cal{O}_A \otimes \sigma^X \sigma^Z
   733	  = (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X)^\dagger.
   734	  \end{equation}
   735	  As a result, this matrix is Hermitian. In addition, 
   736	  \begin{equation*}
   737	  (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X)^2
   738	  = (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X) \cdot (\cal{O}_B \cal{O}_A \otimes \sigma^X \sigma^Z)
   739	  = (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \cdot \cal{O}_B \cal{O}_A) \otimes (\sigma^Z \sigma^X \cdot \sigma^X \sigma^Z)
   740	  = I,
   741	  \end{equation*}
   742	  where the first step uses Equation~\eqref{eq:am-i-hermitian} and the final
   743	  step uses the fact that $\cal{O}_A, \cal{O}_B, \sigma^X, \sigma^Z$ are $\pm
   744	  1$-valued observables and hence square to the identity.
   745	  As a result, this matrix is Hermitian and squares to the identity.
   746	  Therefore, it is a $\pm 1$-valued observable.
   747	  
   748	  As for the $\Constraint_i$ measurements,
   749	  we must show that the three measurements in each row and column are simultaneously measurable.
   750	  This is equivalent to the three $\pm 1$-valued observables being simultaneously diagonalizable,
   751	  which is equivalent to them being pairwise commuting. This can be easily verified for the cases of $i = 1, 2, 4, 5$
   752	  (i.e.\ the first two rows and columns).
   753	  In the case of $i = 3$, commutativity of $\cal{O}_A \otimes \sigma^Z$ and $\cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^X$ 
   754	  follows from Equation~\eqref{eq:am-i-hermitian}.
   755	  Since these two matrices commute, they also commute with their product 
   756	  $(\cal{O}_A \otimes \sigma^Z)(\cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^X) = \cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X$.
   757	  The case of $i = 6$ is similar.
   758	  
   759	  By construction, $\strategy$ is symmetric, and we have already shown that it
   760	  is projective.
   761	  It remains to show that it is commuting, consistent, and value~$1$.
   762	  To show that it is commuting, it suffices to show that the measurement for
   763	  each cell is simultaneously measurable with all three measurements in its row
   764	  or column, which was already proved above.
   765	  Now we show consistency of the measurements.
   766	  We will show this by instead showing consistency of their observables.
   767	  By this we mean the following: if $E = \{E_0, E_1\}$ is a two-outcome projective measurement on $\cal{H}$
   768	  then its corresponding $\pm 1$-valued observable $\cal{O} = E_0 - E_1$
   769	  is consistent on a state $\ket{\phi} \in \cal{H} \otimes \cal{H}$ if
   770	  \begin{equation*}
   771	  \cal{O}\otimes I_{\bob} \cdot \ket{\phi} = I_{\alice} \otimes \cal{O} \cdot \ket{\phi}.
   772	  \end{equation*}
   773	  This is in fact equivalent to the notion of $E$ being consistent on $\ket{\phi}$ from Definition~\ref{def:consistent-measurement}.
   774	  To see this, if $E$ is consistent on $\ket{\phi}$, then so is $\cal{O}$, because
   775	  \begin{equation*}
   776	  \cal{O}\otimes I_{\bob} \cdot \ket{\phi}
   777	  = (E_0 - E_1) \otimes I_{\bob} \cdot \ket{\phi}
   778	  = I_{\alice} \otimes (E_0 - E_1) \cdot \ket{\phi}
   779	  = I_{\alice} \otimes \cal{O} \cdot \ket{\phi},
   780	  \end{equation*}
   781	  where the second equality is by consistency of~$E$.
   782	  On the other hand, suppose $\cal{O}$ is consistent on $\ket{\phi}$.
   783	  Then because $E_0 + E_1 = I$, we can write $E_0 = \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot (I + \cal{O})$ and $E_1 = \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot (I - \cal{O})$.
   784	  As a result,
   785	  \begin{equation*}
   786	  E_0 \otimes I_{\bob} \cdot \ket{\phi}
   787	  = \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot (I + \cal{O}) \otimes I_{\bob} \cdot \ket{\phi}
   788	  = I_{\alice} \otimes \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot (I + \cal{O}) \cdot \ket{\phi}
   789	  = I_{\alice} \otimes E_0 \cdot \ket{\phi},
   790	  \end{equation*}
   791	  and similarly for $E_0$. Thus, $E$ is consistent on $\ket{\phi}$.
   792	  This proves the equivalence.
   793	  
   794	  Now we use this to prove consistency of $\strategy$.
   795	  To begin, we note that because $A$ and $B$ are consistent on $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n}$ by assumption,
   796	  so to are their $\pm 1$-valued observables $\cal{O}_A$ and $\cal{O}_B$.
   797	  Next, we note that $\sigma^X$ and $\sigma^Z$ are consistent on $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$;
   798	  to verify this, we recall that $\sigma^X \ket{0} = \ket{1}$ and $\sigma^X \ket{1} = \ket{0}$, and so
   799	  \begin{align*}
   800	  \sigma^X \otimes I_{\bob} \cdot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}
   801	&  =   \sigma^X \otimes I_{\bob} \cdot \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\ket{00} + \ket{11})\\
   802	&  = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\ket{10} + \ket{01})
   803	    =    I_{\alice} \otimes \sigma^X \cdot \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} (\ket{11} + \ket{00})
   804	    =    I_{\alice} \otimes \sigma^X \cdot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}.
   805	  \end{align*}
   806	  This shows $\sigma^X$ is consistent on $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$,
   807	  and a similar argument shows the same for $\sigma^Z$.
   808	  We now use these two facts to show that the observable in each cell of
   809	  Figure~\ref{fig:ms-operator-soln} is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$.
   810	  To see why, consider the $j = 9$ case:
   811	  \begin{align*}
   812	&  (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X)_\alice \otimes I_\bob
   813			\cdot \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2} \\
   814	  ={}& (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z)_\alice \otimes (I \otimes \sigma^X)_\bob
   815	  		\cdot \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}\tag{consistency of $\sigma^X$}\\
   816	  ={}& (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes I)_\alice \otimes (I \otimes \sigma^X\sigma^Z)_\bob
   817	  		\cdot \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}\tag{consistency of $\sigma^Z$}\\
   818	  ={}& (\cal{O}_A \otimes I)_\alice \otimes ( \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^X\sigma^Z)_\bob
   819	  		\cdot \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}\tag{consistency of $\cal{O}_B$}\\
   820	  ={}& I_\alice \otimes (\cal{O}_B \cal{O}_A \otimes \sigma^X\sigma^Z)_\bob
   821	  		\cdot \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}\tag{consistency of $\cal{O}_A$}\\
   822	  ={}& I_\alice \otimes (\cal{O}_A \cal{O}_B \otimes \sigma^Z \sigma^X)_\bob
   823	  		\cdot \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes n} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}. \tag{by Equation~\eqref{eq:am-i-hermitian}}
   824	  \end{align*}
   825	  The remaining cases of $j \in\{1, \ldots, 8\}$ are similar, and we omit them.
   826	  This shows that the observable in each cell is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$,
   827	  and as a result the corresponding two-outcome projective measurements are consistent as well.
   828	  As a result, the $\Variable_j$ measurements are consistent.
   829	  
   830	  As for the $\Constraint_i$ measurements, each such measurement $\{F_{a, b,
   831	    c}\}_{a, b, c \in \{0, 1\}}$ is of the form $F_{a, b, c} = E^1_a \cdot E^2_b
   832	  \cdot E^3_c$, where $E^1$, $E^2$, and $E^3$ are $\Variable$ measurements.
   833	  But then consistency of~$F$ follows from the~$\Variable$ consistencies:
   834	  \begin{align*}
   835	  F_{a, b, c} \otimes I_{\bob} \ket{\psi}
   836	 & = (E^1_a \cdot E^2_b \cdot E^3_c)_{\alice} \otimes I_{\bob} \ket{\psi}\\
   837	 & = (E^1_a \cdot E^2_b)_{\alice} \otimes (E^3_c)_{\bob} \ket{\psi} \tag{consistency of $E^3$}\\
   838	 &   = (E^1_a)_{\alice} \otimes (E^3_c \cdot E^2_b)_{\bob} \ket{\psi}\tag{consistency of $E^2$}\\
   839	 &       = I_{\alice} \otimes (E^3_c \cdot E^2_b \cdot E^1_a)_{\bob} \ket{\psi}\tag{consistency of $E^1$}\\
   840	 &       = I_{\alice} \otimes (E^1_a \cdot E^2_b \cdot E^2_c)_{\bob} \ket{\psi}\tag{commutativity of $E^1$, $E^2$, and $E^3$}\\
   841	 &               = I_{\alice} \otimes F_{a, b,c} \ket{\psi}.
   842	  \end{align*}
   843	  Hence, all measurements are consistent.
   844	  
   845	  Since all measurements are consistent, this implies that the answer bit of the
   846	  player receiving a $\Variable$ question is always consistent with the
   847	  corresponding answer bit of the player receiving the $\Constraint$ question.
   848	  Similarly, the answers of the player receiving the $\Constraint$ question
   849	  always satisfy the given constraint; observe that in all rows and the first
   850	  two columns, the observables multiply to $I$, whereas the observables in the
   851	  last column multiply to $-I$.
   852	  This implies that the strategy is value-$1$.
   853	  To see why, 
   854	  let us again consider a $\Constraint_i$ measurement, which we write as $F=\{F_{a, b, c}\}_{a, b, c \in \{0, 1\}}$.
   855	  As above, it can be written as  $F_{a, b, c} = E^1_a \cdot E^2_b \cdot E^3_c$, where $E^1$, $E^2$, and $E^3$ are $\Variable$ measurements.
   856	  Consider the measurement $S=\{S_0, S_1\}$ that corresponds to measuring $\{F_{a, b, c}\}$ and then outputting the sum of measured values of~$a$, $b$, and~$c$.
   857	  In other words,
   858	  \begin{equation*}
   859	  S_0 = F_{0, 0, 0} + F_{0, 1, 1} + F_{1, 0, 1} + F_{1, 1, 0},
   860	  \qquad
   861	  S_1 = F_{0, 0, 1} + F_{0, 1, 0} + F_{1, 0, 0} + F_{1, 1, 1}.
   862	  \end{equation*}
   863	  The following expression gives a convenient formula for the $\pm 1$-valued observable $S_0 - S_1$:
   864	  \begin{equation*}
   865	  (E_0^1 - E_1^1) \cdot (E_0^2 - E_1^2) \cdot (E_0^3 - E_1^3)
   866	  = E_0^1 E_0^2 E_0^3 - E_0^1 E_0^2 E_1^3 - E_0^1 E_1^2 E_0^3 + E_0^1 E_1^2 E_1^3 + \cdots
   867	  = S_0 - S_1.
   868	  \end{equation*}
   869	  When we are looking at $\Constraint_i$ for $i \in \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$,
   870	  the left-hand side of this equation is equal to $I$, and so $I = S_0- S_1$.
   871	  Because $S_0$ and $S_1$ are both positive semidefinite,
   872	  this is true only if $S_0 = I$ and $S_1 = 0$, which implies that the three bits output by $F$ always sum to~$0$.
   873	  As a result, this strategy always satisfies the $\Constraint_i$ question.
   874	  On the other hand, when $i = 6$, then the left-hand side of this equation is equal to $-I$,
   875	  and so $S_1 = I$, and the three bits sum to~$1$.
   876	  Thus, the strategy always satisfies the $\Constraint_6$ question as well.
   877	  This concludes the proof.
   878	\end{proof}

   880	\subsection{The Pauli basis test}
   881	\label{sec:pauli-verifier}
   882	
   883	We introduce the quantum low-degree test of~\cite{natarajan2018low} in the form
   884	of a slight modification to it by~\cite{NW19} known as the \emph{Pauli basis
   885	  test}.
   886	Informally, the quantum low-degree test asks the players to measure a large
   887	number of qubits and return a highly compressed version of the measurement
   888	outcome.
   889	The Pauli basis test simply asks that the players return their uncompressed
   890	measurement outcomes, and it is designed by direct reduction to the quantum
   891	low-degree test.
   892	In Section~\ref{sec:qld-game} we describe the Pauli basis test as a nonlocal
   893	game $\game^\pauli$ and show that its question distribution is implementable via
   894	a CL distribution, as we did with the classical low-degree test in
   895	Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   896	In Section~\ref{sec:qld-complexity} we exhibit canonical parameters for the
   897	Pauli basis test and give bounds on the time complexity of executing the test.
   898	
   899	\subsubsection{The game}
   900	\label{sec:qld-game}
   901	
   902	We start by discussing parameter settings.
   903	The game $\game^\pauli$ is parametrized by a tuple
   904	\[\qldparams = (q,m,d)\;,\] where $q,m,d \in \N$ are integers. 
   905	We sometimes write $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
   906	Pauli basis test on the parameters.
   907	
   908	Informally, the test is meant to certify that the players share a state of the
   909	form $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}$, where $M=2^m$.
   910	Its question set includes questions that are axis-parallel/diagonal lines and points in $\F_q^m$,
   911	which are meant to correspond to questions in the classical low-degree test, and questions
   912	of the form $(\Pauli, W)$, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   913	Upon receipt of a question of the latter form, the players are expected to
   914	perform the POVM $\{\tau_h^W\}_{h \in \F_q^{M}}$ and report the outcome $h$ as
   915	their answer.
   916	
   917	The key idea behind the test
   918	is for the provers to encode their outcomes using the \emph{low-degree encoding} from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}.
   919	Given an outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, the low-degree encoding of~$h$ is the polynomial $g_h:\F_q^m \rightarrow \F_q$.
   920	Rather than asking the provers to always return the entire string~$h$,
   921	many of the subtests in the game $\game^\pauli$ will ``probe'' limited information about~$h$ as follows:
   922	the verifier provides the provers with a string $u_W \in \F_q^m$,
   923	and using this they are expected to evaluate $g_h(u_W) \in \F_q$ and return it to the verifier.
   924	For a fixed value of~$W$, then, the prover's responses to these ``probes'' should be consistent with some low-degree polynomial in the input~$u_W$.
   925	To check this, the verifier can perform the classical low-degree test from Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   926	This ensures that the prover's responses for the $W = X$ basis are consistent with each other,
   927	as well as their responses for the $W = Z$ basis, although it does not test consistency between the $X$ and $Z$ responses.
   928	
   929	The next set of subtests the verifier performs ensure that the provers' $X$ and $Z$ measurements are consistent with each other.
   930	On the $X$ side, consider the measurement in which the prover performs the $\{\tau_h^X\}$ POVM,
   931	receives outcome $h_X$, and outputs $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$.
   932	For technical reasons that will become clear shortly,
   933	it will be convenient for the prover's measurement to have two outcomes rather than~$q$ outcomes.
   934	To accomplish this, the verifier also provides the prover with an element $r_X \in \F_q$;
   935	given this, the prover should output not $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$ but $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$, which is an element of $\F_2$.
   936	Similarly, on the $Z$ side, suppose the prover is provided $r_Z \in \F_q$,
   937	performs $\{\tau_h^Z\}$ to receive $h_Z$, and outputs $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z) \in \F_2$.
   938	Together, these two are a pair of two-outcome measurements, one in the~$X$ basis and one in the~$Z$ basis,
   939	and as it turns out, this pair of measurements either commutes with each other or anticommutes with each other
   940	(this is why we modified the measurements to have only two outcomes).
   941	The key quantity to determine which of these is the case is the following complicated-looking expression:
   942	\begin{equation*}
   943	\gamma = \tr \bigl( (\ind_{m}(u_\xpt) \cdot r_\xpt) \cdot
   944	      (\ind_{m}(u_\zpt) \cdot r_\zpt) \bigr)\;.
   945	\end{equation*}
   946	If $\gamma = 0$, then these two measurements commute, and if $\gamma = 1$, then these two measurements anticommute
   947	(this fact is established in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-completeness} below).
   948	In the $\gamma = 0$ case, the verifier can check whether these two measurements commute by performing the ``commutation check'',
   949	which asks the provers to simultaneously measure both $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$ and $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z)$ and report their values.
   950	In the $\gamma = 1$ case, on the other hand, the measurements anticommute, which implies that they cannot simultaneously be measured.
   951	In spite of this, the verifier can still check that the measurements anticommute by using the Magic Square game from Section~\ref{sec:ms} above.
   952	As was shown in Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, any pair of anticommuting measurements
   953	can be used to form a perfect strategy for the Magic Square game
   954	(and indeed the reverse is true as well: any perfect strategy for the Magic Square game entails a pair of anticommuting measurements).
   955	
   956	Together, these give the main subtests for the game $\game^\pauli$.
   957	
   958	\begin{definition}[Admissible parameters]\label{def:admissible}
   959	  We say that the tuple $\qldparams=(q, m, d)$ is \emph{admissible} if $q$ is
   960	  an admissible field size (Definition~\ref{def:admissible-size}) and $m | q$.
   961	\end{definition}
   962	
   963	
   964	\paragraph{Question distribution.}
   965	We now describe the question distribution of the game $\game^\pauli$, and show
   966	that it is a (typed) CL distribution.
   967	The question types in the game $\game^\pauli$ are
   968	\begin{equation}
   969	  \label{eq:pauli-type}
   970	  \type^\pauli= \bigl( \{\Point, \ALine, \DLine, \Pauli, \Pair \} \times \{X,Z\} \bigr)
   971	  \cup \type^\ms \cup \{\Pair\}\;,
   972	\end{equation}
   973	where $\type^\ms$ is the question type set of the Magic Square game defined in
   974	Section~\ref{sec:ms}.
   975	
   976	
   977	
   978	
   979	Before presenting the CL functions of the Pauli basis test, we first give an
   980	intuitive description of the question distribution of the Pauli basis test: a
   981	pair of questions $((\tvar_\alice, x_\alice), (\tvar_\bob, x_\bob))$ in
   982	$\game^\pauli$ can be sampled via the following procedure:
   983	
   984	\begin{enumerate}
   985	\item Sample a pair of types by sampling an edge $(\tvar_\alice, \tvar_\bob)$ of
   986	  the graph $G^\pauli$ given in Figure~\ref{fig:type-graph-pauli} uniformly at
   987	  random (including the self-loops).
   988	\item Sample the following uniformly at random:
   989		\begin{enumerate}
   990		\item (\emph{Points}) $u_\xpt,u_\zpt \in \F_q^m$,
   991		\item (\emph{Directions}) $s \in \F_q$, $v \in \F_q^m$,
   992	  \item (\emph{Qubit basis for (anti-)commutation}) $r_\xpt,r_\zpt \in \F_q$.
   993		\end{enumerate}
   994	\item For $w \in \AB$ and $W\in\{X,Z\}$,
   995		\begin{enumerate}
   996	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\Point, W)$, then set $x_w = u_W$,
   997	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\ALine, W)$, then set $x_w = (u_0,s)$, where $u_0 =
   998	    L^\lnf_{e_i}(u_W)$, with $i = \chi(s)$ (see \Cref{sec:ld-game} for
   999	    definition of $L^\lnf$ and $\chi(s)$),
  1000	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\DLine,W)$, then set $x_w = (u_0,s,v')$, where $i =
  1001	    \chi(s)$, $v' = \pi_{i-1}(v)$, and $u_0 = L^\lnf_{v'}(u_W)$,
  1002	  \item If $\tvar_w = \Constraint_i$ for some $i\in\{1,\ldots,6\}$, then set
  1003	    $x_w = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1004	  \item If $\tvar_w = \Variable_j$ for some $j\in\{1,\ldots,9\}$, then set $x_w
  1005	    = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1006	  \item If $\tvar_w = \Pair$, then set $x_w = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1007	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\Pair, W)$, then set $x_w = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1008	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\Pauli, W)$, then set $x_w = 0$.
  1009		\end{enumerate}
  1010	\end{enumerate}

  1073	\paragraph{Conditional linear functions for the Pauli basis test.}
  1074	The CL functions corresponding to the Pauli basis test question distribution are
  1075	parameterized by the parameter tuple $\qldparams = (q,m,d)$.
  1076	Let $V^\pauli$ denote the linear space $(\F_q^m)^2 \times \F_q \times \F_q^m
  1077	\times (\F_q)^2$.
  1078	The space $V^\pauli$ is decomposed into a direct sum of the following register
  1079	subspaces: $V_\xpt,V_\zpt$ (which are $m$-dimensional), $V_\coord$ (which is
  1080	$1$-dimensional), $V_{\dir{}}$ (which is $m$-dimensional), and
  1081	$V_{\rxpt},V_{\rzpt}$ (which are $1$-dimensional).
  1082	We identify elements of $V^\pauli$ as tuples $(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1083	\in (\F_q^m)^2 \times \F_q \times \F_q^m \times (\F_q)^2$.
  1084	We define CL functions $L_\tvar: V^\pauli \to V^\pauli$ for every type $\tvar
  1085	\in \type^\pauli$:
  1086	\begin{enumerate}
  1087	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\Point,W}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1088	  = L_\Point(u_W,s,v)$ where $L_\Point$ is the $1$-level CL function defined in
  1089	  \Cref{eq:cl-ptf}.\footnote{The range $V_{\xpt} \oplus V_\coord \oplus
  1090	    V_{\dir{}}$ or $V_{\zpt} \oplus V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ of $L_\Point$ is
  1091	    embedded in $V^\pauli$ in the natural way.
  1092	    The same convention is used also in Item 2 and 3 for $L_\ALine$ and
  1093	    $L_\DLine$.}
  1094	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\ALine,W}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1095	  = L_\ALine(u_W,s,v)$ where $L_\ALine$ is the $2$-level CL function defined in
  1096	  \Cref{eq:cl-alnf}.
  1097	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\DLine,W}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1098	  = L_\DLine(u_W,s,v)$ where $L_\DLine$ is the $3$-level CL function defined in
  1099	  \Cref{eq:cl-dlnf}.
  1100	\item For $\tvar \in \type^\ms \cup \{\Pair, (\Pair,X), (\Pair,Z) \}$,
  1101	  $L_{\tvar}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt) =
  1102	  (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,0,0,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)$, i.e., it projects onto $V_\xpt \oplus
  1103	  V_\zpt \oplus V_{\rxpt} \oplus V_{\rzpt}$.
  1104	  Thus $L_{\tvar}$ is a $1$-level CL function.
  1105	  
  1106	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\Pauli,W} = 0$ as the identically $0$
  1107	  function.
  1108	  Thus it is a $0$-level CL function.
  1109	
  1110	\end{enumerate}
  1111	We note that the maps $L_{\Point,W}, L_{\ALine,W}, L_{\DLine,W}$ act as the zero function
  1112	on $V_{\overline{W}} \oplus V_{\rxpt} \oplus V_{\rzpt}$ where $\overline{W} = X$
  1113	if $W = Z$ and $\overline{W} = Z$ if $W = X$.
  1114	
  1115	The question distribution of $\game^\pauli$ is thus a typed CL distribution on
  1116	$\type^\pauli \times V^\pauli \times \type^\pauli \times V^\pauli$ where
  1117	$(\tvar_\alice,x_\alice,\tvar_\bob,x_\bob)$ is sampled by first uniformly
  1118	sampling an edge $(\tvar_\alice,\tvar_\bob)$ from the graph $G^\pauli$ defined
  1119	in Figure~\ref{fig:type-graph-pauli}, sampling a uniformly random $z \in
  1120	V^\pauli$, and then setting $x_w = L_{\tvar_w}(z)$ for $w \in \AB$.

  1172	    \begin{enumerate}[itemsep=2pt,parsep=2pt]
  1173	    \item (\textbf{Consistency check}).
  1174	      \label{item:same-type}
  1175	      If $\tvar_\alice = \tvar_\bob$, accept iff $a_\alice = a_\bob$.
  1176	
  1177	    \item (\textbf{Low-degree}).
  1178	      \label{item:low-degree}
  1179	      Let $\ldparams = (q,m,d,1)$. 
  1180	      \begin{enumerate}
  1181	      	\item If $\tvar_w = (\Point, W), \tvar_{\overline{w}} = (\ALine, W)$, accept if
  1182	      $\decider^\ld_{\ldparams}$ accepts $(\Point, x_w, \ALine, x_{\overline{w}}, a_w,
  1183	      a_{\overline{w}})$.
  1184	      	\item If $\tvar_w = (\Point, W), \tvar_{\overline{w}} = (\DLine, W)$, accept if
  1185	      $\decider^\ld_{\ldparams}$ accepts $(\Point, x_w, \DLine, x_{\overline{w}}, a_w,
  1186	      a_{\overline{w}})$.
  1187			\end{enumerate}
  1188	    \item (\textbf{Consistency check}).
  1189	      \label{item:low-degree-consistency}
  1190	      If $\tvar_w = (\Point, W), \tvar_{\overline{w}} = (\Pauli, W)$, accept if
  1191	      $g_{a_{\overline{w}}}(x_w) = a_w$, where $g_{a_{\overline{w}}}$ is
  1192	      the low-degree encoding of $a_{\overline{w}} \in \F_q^M$ defined in

  1198	      \label{eq:gamma-value}
  1199	      \gamma = \tr \bigl( (\ind_{m}(u_\xpt) \cdot r_\xpt) \cdot

  1229	We describe an honest, value-$1$ PCC strategy for the Pauli basis test.
  1230	
  1231	
  1232	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:pauli-completeness}
  1233	  The Pauli basis test $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ has a value-$1$ SPCC strategy.
  1234	\end{lemma}
  1235	
  1236	\begin{proof}
  1237	  We begin by specifying the value-$1$ strategy $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, E)$.
  1238	  The state is
  1239	  \begin{equation*}
  1240	    \ket{\psi} = \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}\;.
  1241	  \end{equation*}
  1242	  Now we specify the measurements.
  1243	  We start with measurements associated with questions of type $\Point$,
  1244	  $\ALine$, $\DLine$, and $\Pauli$.
  1245	  Using notation introduced in Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}, for $W \in \{X,
  1246	  Z\}$,
  1247	  \begin{align*}
  1248	    E^{(\Point,W),\, y}_{\, a}
  1249	    & = \tau^W_{[g_{\cdot}(y) = a]} \otimes I\;,\\
  1250	    E^{(\ALine,W),\, \line}_{\, f}
  1251	    & = \tau^W_{[(g_{\cdot})|_\line = f]} \otimes I\;,\\
  1252	    E^{(\DLine,W),\, \line}_{\, f}
  1253	    & = \tau^W_{[(g_{\cdot})|_\line = f]} \otimes I\;,\\    
  1254	    E^{(\Pauli,W)}_{\, a}
  1255	    & = \tau^W_{a} \otimes I\;.
  1256	  \end{align*}
  1257	  Here, the bracket notation used to post-process measurement outcomes is
  1258	  defined in \Cref{def:bracket}.
  1259	  Thus, for example, the measurement on question $((\Point,W),y)$ corresponds to
  1260	  first performing the measurement $\{\tau^W_h\}_{h \in \F_q^M}$, receiving an
  1261	  outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, and then outputting the value $a = g_{h}(y)$.
  1262	
  1263	  For $\ALine$ and $\DLine$ questions, the question content $\line$ denotes
  1264	  either an axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$ for some $i \in
  1265	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$, or a diagonal line $\line(u_0,v')$ for some $v' \in
  1266	  \F_q^m$.
  1267	  As described at the beginning of \Cref{sec:qld-game}, axis-parallel lines are
  1268	  specified by pairs $(u_0,s) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q$ and diagonal lines are
  1269	  specified by triples $(u_0,s,v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q \times \F_q^m$.
  1270	  The measurement on question $((\ALine,W),\line)$, for example, corresponds to
  1271	  first performing the measurement $\{\tau^W_h\}_{h \in \F_q^M}$ to get an
  1272	  outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, and reporting the univariate polynomial $f_\line(t) =
  1273	  g_{h}(u_0 + te_i)$ where $\line$ is specified by $(u_0,s)$ and $i = \chi(s)$.
  1274	  
  1275	
  1276	
  1277	  Next we specify the POVMs associated with questions of type $\Constraint$,
  1278	  $\Variable$, and $\Pair$.
  1279	  Questions with these question types have a question content that is a tuple
  1280	  $\omega= (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)\in (\F_q^m)^2 \times \F_q^2$.
  1281	  Given such a tuple, consider the two $\F_2$-valued POVMs $A=\{A_b\}_{b \in
  1282	    \F_2}$ and $B=\{B_b\}_{b \in \F_2}$ defined as
  1283	  \begin{align}
  1284	    A_b & = \tau^X_{[\tr(g_{\cdot}(u_X)\, r_\xpt) = b]} \otimes I\;,\label{eq:gonna-expand-A}\\
  1285	    B_b & = \tau^Z_{[\tr(g_{\cdot}(u_Z)\, r_\zpt) = b]} \otimes I\;.\label{eq:gonna-expand-B}
  1286	  \end{align}
  1287	  We would like to determine when the two observables $\mathcal{O}_A = A_0 -
  1288	  A_1$ and $\mathcal{O}_B = B_0 - B_1$ commute or anti-commute.
  1289	  Towards this we derive alternative expressions for these observables from
  1290	  which their commutativity becomes plain from inspection.
  1291	  We begin by inspecting the first matrices on the right-hand sides of
  1292	  Equations~\eqref{eq:gonna-expand-A} and~\eqref{eq:gonna-expand-B}:
  1293	  \begin{align}
  1294	  \tau^W_{[\tr(g_{\cdot}(u_W)\, r_W) = b]}
  1295	  &= \sum_{h : \tr(g_{h}(u_W)\, r_W) = b} \tau^W_h\nonumber\\
  1296	  &= \sum_{h : \tr((h\, \cdot\, \ind_{m}(u_W)) \cdot r_W ) = b} \tau^W_h\;,\label{eq:expand-with-dot-product}
  1297	  \end{align}
  1298	  where~\eqref{eq:expand-with-dot-product}
  1299	  follows by  Definition~\ref{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}.
  1300	  As a result,
  1301	  \begin{align}
  1302	&  \tau^W_{[\tr(g_{\cdot}(u_W)\, r_W) = 0]}
  1303	  -   \tau^W_{[\tr(g_{\cdot}(u_W)\, r_W) = 1]} \notag \\
  1304	  & = \sum_{h : \tr((h\, \cdot\, \ind_{m}(u_W)) \cdot r_W ) = 0} \tau^W_h
  1305	  	- \sum_{h : \tr((h\, \cdot\, \ind_{m}(u_W)) \cdot r_W ) = 1} \tau^W_h\nonumber\\
  1306	  & = \sum_{h} (-1)^{\tr((h\, \cdot\, \ind_{m}(u_W)) \cdot r_W )} \tau^W_h\nonumber\\
  1307	  & = \tau^W(\ind_{m}(u_W)r_W)\;,\label{eq:finally-got-an-observable}
  1308	  \end{align}
  1309	  where the last step uses~\eqref{eq:pauli-obs-proj}.
  1310	  As a result, Equation~\eqref{eq:finally-got-an-observable}
  1311	  and Equations~\eqref{eq:gonna-expand-A} and~\eqref{eq:gonna-expand-B} imply that
  1312	  \begin{equation*}
  1313	  \mathcal{O}_A = \tau^X(\ind_{m}(u_X)r_X) \otimes I,\quad
  1314	  \mathcal{O}_B = \tau^Z(\ind_{m}(u_Z)r_Z) \otimes I\;.
  1315	  \end{equation*}
  1316	  Now, let $\gamma = \tr((\ind_{m}(u_X)r_X) \cdot (\ind_{m}(u_Z)r_Z)) \in \F_2$,
  1317	  as in Equation~\eqref{eq:gamma-value}.
  1318	  Then by Equation~\eqref{eq:twisted-fq},
  1319	  \begin{equation*}
  1320	  \mathcal{O}_A \mathcal{O}_B = (-1)^{\gamma} \mathcal{O}_B \mathcal{O}_A\;.
  1321	  \end{equation*}
  1322	  As a result, $\gamma$ quantifies whether the observables $\mathcal{O}_A$ and
  1323	  $\mathcal{O}_B$ commute, and therefore whether the measurements~$A$ and~$B$
  1324	  commute.
  1325	  If $\gamma = 0$, they commute.
  1326	  If $\gamma = 1$, they anti-commute.
  1327	  We now specify the POVMs associated with questions of type $\Constraint$,
  1328	  $\Variable$, and $\Pair$, considering separately the cases when $\gamma = 0$
  1329	  or $\gamma = 1$.
  1330	  \begin{enumerate}
  1331	  \item If $\gamma = 0$, 
  1332	     for each $\beta_X, \beta_Z \in \F_2$ define
  1333	    \begin{equation}\label{eq:pair-definition}
  1334	      E^{\Pair,\, \omega}_{\beta_X,\, \beta_Z} = A_{\beta_X} \cdot B_{\beta_Z}\;,
  1335	    \end{equation}
  1336	    \begin{equation*}
  1337	      E^{(\Pair,X),\, \omega}_{a} = A_{a} \;,\qquad
  1338	      E^{(\Pair,Z),\, \omega}_{a} = B_{a}\;.
  1339	    \end{equation*}
  1340	    The POVM associated with questions of type $\Constraint$ and $\Variable$ are
  1341	    defined to be trivial.
  1342	    In particular, we define
  1343	    \begin{equation*}
  1344	      E^{\Constraint_i,\, \omega}_{\, 0,\, 0,\, 0}
  1345	      = E^{\Variable_j,\, \omega}_{\, 0} = I\;,
  1346	    \end{equation*}
  1347	    and the remaining POVM elements in these measurements are set to be zero.
  1348	  \item If $\gamma = 1$, then $\mathcal{O}_A$ and $\mathcal{O}_B$ anti-commute.
  1349	    In this case we define measurements $E^{\Constraint_i,\, \omega}$ and
  1350	    $E^{\Variable_j,\, \omega}$, for all $i\in\{1,\ldots,6\}$ and $j
  1351	    \in\{1,\ldots,9\}$ to be those guaranteed by Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}.
  1352	    Measurements associated with inputs of type $\Pair$ are defined to be
  1353	    trivial.
  1354	    In particular, we define
  1355	    \begin{equation*}
  1356	      E^{\Pair,\, \omega}_{0,\, 0} = E^{(\Pair,X),\, \omega}_{0} = E^{(\Pair,Z),\, \omega}_{0} = I\;,
  1357	    \end{equation*}
  1358	    and the remaining matrices in these measurements are set to be zero.
  1359	  \end{enumerate}
  1360	  This completes the specification of the strategy.
  1361	
  1362	  Now, we show that $\strategy$ is a value-$1$ SPCC strategy.
  1363	  It is clearly symmetric and projective. 
  1364	  To show that it is consistent, we note that all measurements are Pauli basis
  1365	  measurements, which are consistent, or measurements produced by
  1366	  Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, which are also consistent.
  1367	  The only exception is the $\Pair$ measurement in the $\gamma = 0$ case, which
  1368	  by Equation~\eqref{eq:pair-definition} is a product of two commuting,
  1369	  consistent measurements, and so it is therefore also consistent.
  1370	  To show that it is commuting, we note that for each $W \in \{X, Z\}$, all
  1371	  $(\Point, W)$, $(\ALine, W)$, $(\DLine,W)$ and $(\Pauli, W)$ measurements
  1372	  commute as they are all measurements in the Pauli~$W$ basis.
  1373	  Next, if $\gamma = 0$ then the $\Constraint$ and $\Variable$ measurements
  1374	  commute trivially, and for $W \in \{X, Z\}$, the $(\Point, W)$ measurement
  1375	  commutes with the $(\Pair, W)$ measurement, as they are both $W$ basis
  1376	  measurements, and the measurement $E^{\Pair, \omega}_{\beta_X, \, \beta_Z} =
  1377	  A_{\beta_X}\cdot B_{\beta_Z}$ commutes with $E^{(\Pair, W), \omega}_{a}$
  1378	  because $A$ and~$B$ commute.
  1379	  On the other hand, if $\gamma \neq 0$, then the $\Pair$ measurements commute
  1380	  trivially, and the $\Constraint$ and $\Variable$ measurements commute by
  1381	  Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}.
  1382	  Finally, the $(\Point, X)$ measurement commutes with $\Variable_1$ because
  1383	  both are $X$-basis measurements, and likewise both $(\Point, Z)$ and
  1384	  $\Variable_5$ are $Z$-basis measurements.
  1385	  
  1386	  It remains to show that $\strategy$ is value-$1$.
  1387		Consider first the first three tests executed by the decision procedure in
  1388	  Figure~\ref{fig:decider_pauli}.
  1389	  The strategy passes the consistency checks with probability~$1$ because it is
  1390	  projective and consistent.
  1391	  It passes the low-degree checks because it answers those consistently with an
  1392	  honest strategy in the classical low-degree test.
  1393			
  1394	  Next, consider the remaining four tests.
  1395	  Fix an $\omega= (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$ and~$\gamma$ as
  1396	  in~\eqref{eq:gamma-value}.
  1397	  If $\gamma = 0$, then the strategy passes the commutation check with
  1398	  probability~$1$ by construction.
  1399	  As for the consistency check in Item~\ref{item:commutation-consistency},
  1400	  we can write the $(\Point, W)$ measurement as follows: 
  1401	  \begin{equation*}
  1402	  E^{(\Point,W),\, y}_{[\tr(\,\cdot\, r_W) = a_{\overline{w}}]}
  1403	  = \tau^W_{[\tr(g_{\cdot}(y)r_W) = a_{\overline{w}}]} \otimes I
  1404	  = E^{(\Pair, W), \omega}_{a_{\overline{w}}} \otimes I.
  1405	  \end{equation*}
  1406	  As a result, due to the consistency of the $(\Pair, W)$ measurement, the
  1407	  consistency check is passed with probability~$1$.
  1408	  On the other hand, if $\gamma \neq 0$, then the strategy passes the Magic
  1409	  Square check by Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}.

  1426	\paragraph{Soundness of the Pauli basis test.} 
  1427	We state the soundness properties of the Pauli basis test.
  1428	The following is an adaptation of the self-testing statement in~\cite[Theorem
  1429	6.4]{NW19}.
  1430	
  1431	\begin{theorem}
  1432	  \label{thm:pauli}
  1433	There exists a function 
  1434	\[\delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})\]
  1435	 for universal constants $a \geq 1$ and $0 < b < 1$ such that the following holds. For all admissible parameter tuples $\qldparams = (q,m,d)$ and for all strategies $\strategy = (\ket{\psi},A,B)$ for the game $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ that succeed with probability at least $1 - \eps$, there exist local isometries $\phi_\alice: \mH_\alice \to \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\alice''},\phi_\bob: \mH_\bob \to \mH_{\bob'} \otimes \mH_{\bob''}$ (where $\ket{\psi} \in \mH_\alice \otimes \mH_\bob$ and $\mH_{\alice''},\mH_{\bob''} \cong (\C^q)^{\otimes M}$ with $M = 2^m$) and a state $\ket{\aux} \in \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\bob'}$ such that 
  1436	\begin{enumerate}
  1437	    \item $\left \| \phi_\alice \otimes \phi_B \ket{\psi} - \ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}  \right \| \leq \delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q)$,
  1438	    \item Letting $\tilde{A}^x_a = \phi_A\, A^x_a \, \phi_A^\dagger$ and $\tilde{B}^y_b = \phi_B B^y_b \phi_B^\dagger$, we have for $W \in \{X,Z\}$
  1439	    \begin{gather*}
  1440	        \tilde{A}^{(\pauli,W)}_u \otimes I_{\bob'\bob''} \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} (\tau^W_u)_{\alice''} \otimes I_{\alice' \bob' \bob''} \\
  1441	        I_{\alice'\alice''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{(\pauli,W)}_u    \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} I_{\alice' \alice'' \bob'} \otimes (\tau^W_u)_{\bob''}\;,
  1442	    \end{gather*}
  1443	    where the $\approx_{\delta_{\qld}}$ statement holds with respect to the state $\ket{\aux}_{\alice'\bob'} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}_{\alice''\bob''}$ and the answer summation is over $u \in \F_q^M$.
  1444	\end{enumerate}
  1445	\end{theorem}

  1492	\subsubsection{Canonical parameters and complexity of the Pauli basis test}
  1493	\label{sec:qld-complexity}
  1494	
  1495	We specify a canonical setting of the parameter tuple $\qldparams$ as a function
  1496	of an integer $R$.
  1497	We call this canonical setting $\introparams$ because we use these in the
  1498	``introspection'' section (\Cref{sec:introspection}).
  1499	We then give bounds on the complexity of computing the decision procedure and CL
  1500	functions of the Pauli basis test corresponding to the parameter tuple
  1501	$\qldparams$, as a function of $R$.
  1502	
  1503	\begin{definition}[Canonical parameters of the Pauli basis test]
  1504	  \label{def:introparams}
  1505	  Let $a,b$ be the universal constants specified in Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli}.
  1506	  Let $c$ denote the smallest even integer that is at least $(b + a)/b$.
  1507	  For all integers $R \geq 4$, define the tuple $\introparams(R) = (q,m,d)$
  1508	  where
  1509	  \begin{itemize}
  1510	  	\item $q = 2^k$ for $k = c \lceil  \log \log R  \rceil + 1$.
  1511		\item $m = 2^j$ where $2^j \leq c \lceil \log R \rceil + 1 < 2^{j+1}$. 
  1512		\item $d = 1$. 
  1513	  \end{itemize}
  1514	\end{definition}
  1515	
  1516	Intuitively, this choice of parameters is such that the Pauli basis test
  1517	certifies the presence of an $M=2^m$-qudit EPR state (of local dimension $q$), or
  1518	equivalently an $M\log q$-qubit EPR state.
  1519	
  1520	\begin{lemma}
  1521	  \label{lem:delta-bound}
  1522	 For all integers $R \geq 4$, the parameter tuple $\introparams(R) = (q,m,d)$ is
  1523	  admissible (see Definition~\ref{def:admissible}), satisfies $2^m \geq R$, and furthermore there exist
  1524	  universal constants $a'\geq 1$ and $0 < b' \leq 1$ such that the function
  1525	  $\delta_\qld(\eps, m, d, q)$ from Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli} is at most
  1526	   \[
  1527	   	a' ( \log(R)^{a'} \cdot \eps^{b'} + \log(R)^{-b'}) \;.
  1528		\]
  1529	\end{lemma}
  1530	
  1531	\begin{proof}
  1532	  We verify the admissibility of $\introparams(R)$ first: the field size $q =
  1533	  2^k$ is admissible because $k$ is odd. We have $m | q$ because for all $R \geq 4$ we have  
  1534	  \[
  1535	  	2^j \leq 2 c \lceil \log R \rceil \leq 2 \log^c R \leq 2^k~.
  1536	  \]
  1537		Next, we show that $R \leq 2^m$. Since $m = 2^j \geq (c/2) \log R$, we have that
  1538		\[
  1539			2^m \geq R^{c/2} \geq R
  1540		\]
  1541		where we used that $c \geq 2$. 
  1542	
  1543	Finally, we show the desired bound on the error function $\delta_\qld(\eps,m,d,q)$. First, observe that $2^{-bmd} \leq q^{-b}$ because $k \leq m$.
  1544	  Note that for $R \geq 2$, we have $m \leq 2c \log R$, and furthermore $q =
  1545	  2^k \geq \log^c R$.
  1546	Then, we get
  1547	\begin{align*}
  1548	  	\delta_\qld(\eps,m,d,q)
  1549	    & = a (md)^a (\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd}) \tag{by Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli}}  \\
  1550	    & \leq a (md)^a (\eps^b + 2q^{-b}) \tag{because  $2^{-bmd} \leq q^{-b}$}  \\
  1551	    & = a (m)^a (\eps^b + 2q^{-b}) \tag{because  $d=1$}  \\
  1552	    & \leq a (2c)^a \log^{a} (R) ( \eps^{b} + 2q^{-b}) \tag{because  $m \leq 2c \log R$}\\
  1553	    & \leq a (2c)^a \log^{a} (R) ( \eps^{b} + 2(\log R)^{-cb}) \tag{because  $q \geq \log^c R$}\\
  1554	    & \leq 2a (2c)^a \log^{a} (R) ( \eps^{b} + (\log R)^{-cb}) \\
  1555	    & = 2a (2c)^a ( (\log R)^{a}\eps^{b} + (\log R)^{a-cb}) \\
  1556	    & \leq 2a(2c)^{a} \left ( (\log R)^{a} \eps^{b}
  1557	      + (\log R)^{-b} \right) \tag{because  $cb - a \geq b \geq 0$}\\
  1558	    & \leq a' ( (\log R)^{a'} \eps^{b} + (\log R)^{-b}),
  1559	  \end{align*}
  1560	  where $a'$ is defined as the quantity $2a(2c)^a$.
  1561	This completes the proof of the lemma.
  1562	\end{proof}
  1563	
  1564	\begin{lemma}
  1565		\label{lem:introparams-complexity}
  1566		Fix an integer $R \geq 4$, let $\introparams(R) = (q,m,d)$.
  1567		The integers $(q,m,d) = \introparams(R)$ can be computed in time $\polylog
  1568	  R$ when given the binary representation of $R$ as input.
  1569	\end{lemma}
  1570	\begin{proof}
  1571	  This follows from the definitions of the parameters in
  1572	  Definition~\ref{def:introparams}.
  1573	  
  1574	\end{proof}
  1575	
  1576	\begin{lemma}
  1577	  \label{lem:qld-complexity}
  1578	  Let $R \geq 4$ be an integer, and let $\introparams(R)$ denote the parameter tuple
  1579	  specified by Definition~\ref{def:introparams}.
  1580	  \begin{enumerate}
  1581		\item The time complexity of the decision procedure $\decider^\pauli$
  1582	    parameterized by $\introparams(R)$ is $\poly(R)$.
  1583		\item The time complexity of computing marginals of the CL functions $L_\tvar$
  1584	    as well as the associated factor spaces, for $\tvar \in \type^\pauli$, is
  1585	    $\polylog R$.
  1586		\item The Turing machine description of the decision procedure
  1587	    $\decider^\pauli$ parameterized by $\introparams$ can be computed from the
  1588	    binary presentation of $R$ in $\polylog (R)$ time.
  1589	  \end{enumerate}
  1590	\end{lemma}
  1591	
  1592	\begin{proof}
  1593		Finite field arithmetic over $\F_q$ can be performed in time $\polylog q$, by
  1594	  Lemma~\ref{lem:efficient_arithmetic}.
  1595	  The parameters of $\introparams(R)$, which the decision procedure
  1596	  $\decider^\pauli$ implicitly computes given $R$, can be computed in time
  1597	  $\polylog(R)$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:introparams-complexity}.
  1598	  The most expensive step in $\decider^\pauli$ is to evaluate the low-degree
  1599	  encoding $g_{a}(y)$ where $a \in \F_q^M$ and $y \in \F_q^m$, which
  1600	  takes time $\poly(M,\log q) = \poly(R)$ by \Cref{lem:ld-encoding-complexity}.
  1601		
  1602	  The complexity of computing the CL functions $L_\tvar$ for types $\tvar \in
  1603	  \type^\pauli$ is dominated by the complexity of computing the CL functions
  1604	  $L_\ALine$, $L_\DLine$, and $L_\Point$ from the classical low-degree test, which takes time
  1605	  $\poly(m, \log q) = \polylog(R)$.
  1606	
  1607	  The factor spaces of $L_\tvar$ depend only on the question type $\tvar$ (of
  1608	  which there are only constantly many), and outputting the length-$m$ indicator
  1609	  vectors of the factor spaces takes $O(m) = \polylog (R)$ time.
  1610	
  1611	  Finally, the time complexity of computing the description of $\decider^\pauli$
  1612	  from the binary representation of $R$ requires $\polylog R$ time, because the
  1613	  checks performed in the decision procedure $\decider^\pauli$ depend on
  1614	  $\introparams$ which ultimately depends on $R$; we assume that the decision
  1615	  procedure computes the parameter tuple $\introparams$ based on $R$.
  1616	  Thus the time complexity is dominated by the time to write $R$ in binary.
  1617	\end{proof}

The following two lemmas establish that the CL functions
$L_\Point,L_\ALine,L_\DLine$ give rise to the axis-parallel line-versus-point and
diagonal line-versus-point distributions.
\begin{lemma}
	\label{lem:alnf}
	Consider the pair $(\line, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
  tuple $((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$,
  and let $\line = \line(u_0,e_i)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a line that
  goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \in
  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
	Since $s$ is uniformly random in $\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$ by assumption, we
  have that $i$ is uniformly random between $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and therefore
  $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$.
  Since $u_0 = L^{\lnf}_{e_i}(u)$, we have that $u \in \line(u_0,e_i)$.
\end{proof}



\begin{lemma}
	\label{lem:dlnf}
	Consider the pair $(\line,u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
  tuple $((u_0,s,v),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$,
  and let $\line = \line(u_0,v)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a random
  diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares the first $i-1$ coordinates
  with $u$, for uniformly random $i$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
	The proof of this follows identically to \Cref{lem:alnf}.
\end{proof}

For later convenience we make the following definition. 

\begin{definition}[Line-point distributions]
        \label{def:line-point-dist}
 The \emph{axis line-point distribution} $D_{\ALine}$ is the
 distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$ over pairs $(\ell=(u_0,e_i),u)$
 (we omit the $0$ elements for simplicity). The \emph{diagonal
   line-point distribution} $D_{\DLine}$ is the distribution
 $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$  over $(\ell=(u_0,s,v),u)$. The
 \emph{line-point distribution} $D_{\Line}$ is the equal mixture of the axis-parallel line-point distribution and the diagonal line-point distribution.
 In other words, a sample from $D_{\Line}$ is distributed as follows:
 with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\ALine}$,
 and with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\DLine}$.
\end{definition}

\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
	Fix $u' \in \line(u,v)$.
  We have that $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$.
  Let $a \in \line(u,v)$.
  This means that $a = u + sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$.
  We also have that $a = u + (s - t + t)v = u + tv + (s - t)v = u' + (s - t)v$,
  so $\line(u,v) \subseteq \line(u',v)$.
  A similar argument shows that $\line(u',v) \subseteq \line(u,v)$.
\end{proof}

We now specify a canonical representation of lines $\line = \line(u,v)$ as pairs $(u_0,v)$
where $u_0$ is a \emph{canonical representative} of $\line$ specified as
follows.
Let $L_v^{\lnf}: \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with the
one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$ (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical} for a
definition of canonical linear map).
Note that for all $u \in \line$, we have that $L_v^{\lnf}(u)$ is a point in
$\line$.
This is because since the image and kernel of $L_v^{\lnf}$ are complementary
subspaces by definition (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical}), any $u \in \F_q^m$ has a
unique decomposition $u = u_0 + u_1$ where $u_0$ is in the image of $L_v^{\lnf}$
and $u_1 \in \ker(L_v^{\lnf})$, which by definition is the subspace spanned by
$v$.
Thus $u_1 = tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$ and we have that $u_0 = u - tv \in \line$.
In particular, if $u\in \line$ then $u_0 = L_v^{\lnf}(u) \in \line$ as well. 
Furthermore, since $L_v^{\lnf}$ is a projection onto its image by definition, we
have $L_v^{\lnf}(u_0) = u_0$.

Next, note that for any $u,u' \in \line$, since $u-u' = sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$
it follows that $L_v^\lnf(u) = L_v^\lnf(u')$.
Thus $u_0 = u_0'$ and this shows that $L_v^\lnf$ gives a means to compute a
canonical representative of lines.

\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]
  \label{def:line-representative}
  Let $\line$ be a line in direction $v$.
  A canonical representative of $\line$ is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
  \[
    u_0 = L_v^\lnf(u)
  \]
  for all $u \in \line$.
\end{definition}

abbrev LdIndex (P : LdParams) := (Fin P.m ⊕ Unit) ⊕ Fin P.m

/-- The full ambient low-degree coefficient space (`def:ld-game`, blueprint
`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`; paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`).

abbrev LdSpace (P : LdParams) := LdIndex P → ScalarQ P

/-- The point coordinates of an ambient low-degree vector in
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
-/
def LdSpace.point {P : LdParams} (z : LdSpace P) : Fin P.m → ScalarQ P :=

/-- The shared scalar coordinate of an ambient low-degree vector in
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
-/
def LdSpace.seed {P : LdParams} (z : LdSpace P) : ScalarQ P :=
  z (.inl (.inr ()) )

/-- The direction coordinates of an ambient low-degree vector in
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
-/
def LdSpace.direction {P : LdParams} (z : LdSpace P) : Fin P.m → ScalarQ P :=
  fun i => z (.inr i)

/-- The integer-coordinate map `χ` from the fixed field representation.  This
is `eq:chi-func` in `def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.

noncomputable def chiIndex (P : LdParams) (s : ScalarQ P) : Fin P.m := by
  letI : NeZero P.m := ⟨by
    exact Nat.ne_of_gt (lt_of_lt_of_le Nat.zero_lt_one P.hm)⟩
  exact Fin.ofNat P.m ((binaryRepresentation P.model s).val / (P.q / P.m))

/-- The projection used in the diagonal-line map zeroes coordinates before the
chosen index and retains the suffix of the direction vector.  This is the
prefix restriction in `def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
-/
def prefixProjection {P : LdParams} (i : Fin P.m) (v : Fin P.m → ScalarQ P) :
    Fin P.m → ScalarQ P :=
  fun j => if j.val < i.val then 0 else v j

/-- The point CL map, retaining the point block and clearing the auxiliary
blocks.  It is the map `L_point` of `def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
-/
def ldPointCL (P : LdParams) (z : LdSpace P) : LdSpace P :=
  fun i => match i with
  | .inl (.inl j) => z (.inl (.inl j))
  | .inl (.inr _) => 0
  | .inr _ => 0

/-- The affine-line CL map.  The direction block is put through the canonical
line representative map from `def:line-representative`, while the point block
is retained (blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`; paper
origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`).
-/
noncomputable def ldALineCL (P : LdParams) (z : LdSpace P) : LdSpace P :=
  let i := chiIndex P (z.seed)
  let rep := lineRepMap (coordinateDirection i)
  fun i => match i with
  | .inl (.inl j) => (rep (z.point)) j
  | .inl (.inr _) => z (.inl (.inr ()))
  | .inr _ => 0

/-- The diagonal-line CL map, using the same canonical representative interface
for the direction block.  This is the `L_DLine` clause of
`def:ld-question-distribution` (blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`; paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`).
-/
noncomputable def ldDLineCL (P : LdParams) (z : LdSpace P) : LdSpace P :=
  let i := chiIndex P (z.seed)
  let direction := prefixProjection i (z.direction)
  let rep := lineRepMap direction
  fun i => match i with
  | .inl (.inl j) => (rep (z.point)) j
  | .inl (.inr _) => z (.inl (.inr ()))
  | .inr j => direction j

/-- Dispatch the three low-degree CL maps by question type.  This is the typed
construction in `def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
-/
noncomputable def ldCL (P : LdParams) : LdType → LdSpace P → LdSpace P
  | .point => ldPointCL P
  | .aline => ldALineCL P
  | .dline => ldDLineCL P

\title{Documenting Possible Gaps, Counterexamples, and Formalization Deviations}
\author{}
\date{2026-04-29}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\section{Purpose}

When a formalization relies on a cited mathematical source, the cited source
should remain intact.  It is a source, not an errata file.  If a possible gap,
missing hypothesis, incorrect numerical constant, or other mathematical
discrepancy is found, the matter should be recorded in a separate LaTeX note.
In this repository such notes live under \path{docs/paper-gaps/}.  The same
principle applies when the formal development has already diverged from the
cited source, for instance by changing a statement so that it compiles, or by
using a different mathematical route because an available formal-library theorem
has a slightly different form.  Such a note is a mathematical note first, and a
record of the formalization second: it should be readable by a mathematician or
mathematical physicist who has not followed the issue discussion.

The note should isolate the mathematical mechanism.  It should say what the
cited source asserts, what the cited results actually imply, where a term or
hypothesis is lost, and what statement the formal development proves instead.
If the formal proof takes a different route, the note should explain the
replacement argument and the hypotheses on which it rests.  This is especially
important when the proof uses a theorem, construction, or convention from
Mathlib which is not part of the cited argument.  In that case the note should
state the Mathlib result in ordinary mathematical language, explain how it is
specialized to the notation of the paper, and compare its hypotheses and
conclusion with the step it replaces.  It should not merely say that \Lean{} did
not accept a proof, that the modified proof compiles, or that a named library
lemma was applied.

The documents in this directory should themselves follow this standard.  A
policy or template which reads like a checklist will tend to produce checklist
notes; the examples and templates should therefore be written as mathematical
prose.

\section{Concision and Readability}

A paper-gap note should be short enough that a reader can understand the issue
in one sitting.  The first page should answer four questions: what the source
uses, how hard the remaining formal work is, what the formalization or audit
checked, and what the current verdict is.  Begin with a short
\emph{At a glance} section when the note concerns an open or recently resolved
formalization task.  That section should estimate the difficulty, the rough
implementation weight, the split between Mathlib reuse and project-local work,
and the key Mathlib APIs or modules.  Use honest ranges, not false precision.

The \emph{Key theorem forms} section should be Section~2, immediately after
\emph{At a glance}.  Put the theorem forms before the source details so the
reader knows what the formalization is aiming to prove.  After that, keep the
source assertion, the mechanism being checked, the blueprint/formal comparison,
and the conclusion.  Use more sections only when a counterexample or long
derivation genuinely needs room.

Keep background to the minimum needed for the local point.  Prefer one clear
special case over a general restatement of the surrounding theorem.  Use displayed
equations for the source assertion, the key calculation, and the theorem forms;
avoid displays for traceability data, declaration names, or long lists.  The
blueprint/formal comparison should be compact and should not repeat the theorem
forms.  The section ``Form of the Note'' below specifies where traceability data
belongs; the body should read as mathematical prose, not as a log.

If the verdict is that there is no mathematical discrepancy, say so plainly and
stop.  Keep the conclusion highly compact, normally under twenty source lines.
If the only remaining work is an implementation task, name it briefly and link
the issue or pull request in a footnote.

\section{When the Investigation Starts}

The investigation starts when the obstruction appears to be mathematical rather
than merely formal.  No final judgement is needed at this stage.  It is enough
that, after reading the relevant source and attempting the corresponding formal
statement, the proof seems to require a different scalar, an additional
hypothesis, a different tensor placement, a distinction between two objects which
the prose identifies, or an auxiliary assertion not supplied by the cited
argument.

The same investigation should also start when such a deviation is discovered
after the fact.  If the existing formal development or informal blueprint has
already changed the statement, strengthened a hypothesis, weakened a conclusion,
inserted an unadvertised lemma, or replaced the cited proof by a different
formal-library argument, the mathematical change should be documented even if all
relevant files already compile.

At this early stage the purpose is to preserve the question while it is still
local.  The note may later conclude that the matter is only notational, that an
intermediate estimate in the cited source needs a harmless correction, that a
missing hypothesis is genuinely needed, or that no discrepancy remains.  Thus
the trigger is not the severity of the eventual verdict, but the appearance of a
real mismatch between the cited reasoning and the statement that can be
formalized.

A failed tactic search, a missing formal lemma, or an inconvenient coercion is
not enough.  The obstruction must survive translation back into ordinary
mathematics.

Sometimes an investigation uncovers an improvement that is not a discrepancy:
the formalization works correctly, but it could be simplified by using an
existing library, replacing a custom type, or adopting a cleaner proof route.
These are not, by themselves, paper-gap notes.  They are action items.  When
such an improvement is identified, open a GitHub issue or pull request that
describes the proposed change.  If the investigation also produces a paper-gap
note, link the issue or pull request from that note: the note records the
mathematical justification, and the issue or pull request drives the
implementation.

\section{When to Write a Note}

A note should be written once the source argument and the formal proof no longer
match as mathematical arguments.  This includes, for instance, a numerical
estimate whose constant does not follow from the cited lemma, a displayed
conclusion which uses an unstated hypothesis, or a step in which two objects are
identified although they must remain distinct.  In analytic, algebraic,
probabilistic, or quantum arguments, such distinctions may concern the domain of
a map, the placement of a tensor factor, the type of an outcome, the distinction
between a structure and a substructure, or the scalar carried by an approximation
relation.

A note is required when an audit finds that a Lean declaration associated with a
source-labelled statement has acquired an extra non-source hypothesis, such as
bridge, residual, repair, producer, or obligation-structure data.  Such a
declaration is temporary proof debt, not a replacement for the source theorem,
and should not be introduced merely to avoid a \verb|sorry|.  The note must say
plainly that the Lean result is conditional, identify the source-faithful theorem
form that remains to be proved, and give the intended obligation discharger or
removal plan.  The blueprint should not mark the source-labelled statement with
\verb|\leanok| by pointing to this conditional helper.

Changing a Lean theorem away from the statement in
\path{references/ldt-paper/} is strongly discouraged.  A paper-gap note should
not make such a change look routine: it should explain the mathematical
necessity, or else classify the change as proof debt to be removed.

When an existing conditional helper is audited, the first task is to extract any
argument it already contains into source-faithful lemmas.  If the remaining
bridge hypothesis cannot be derived from the paper hypotheses, the formal
development should restore the source theorem statement and record the missing
proof obligation explicitly, rather than retaining the strengthened statement as
though it were the paper theorem.

This requirement is not meant to classify every explicit Lean side condition as
a discrepancy.  Positivity, nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances,
and denominator nonvanishing hypotheses may be faithful encodings of the domain
in which the paper's theorem is stated.  The note should distinguish such
boundary hypotheses from hypotheses that supply an unproved step of the paper
argument.

A note is also appropriate when the proof becomes formal only after changing an
intermediate scalar, weakening a conclusion, strengthening a hypothesis, or
inserting an additional lemma which is not simply an expansion of the cited
argument.  These are mathematical changes, even when they are harmless for the
final theorem.  It is likewise appropriate when an available formal-library
theorem proves the needed result under a somewhat different formulation from the
cited source.  In that case the note should be deliberately pedagogical.  It
should explain, in ordinary mathematical language, what the replacement result
says, how it is specialized, which hypotheses are new or differently packaged,
and why the resulting statement is a legitimate substitute for the step in the
cited argument.  If the issue remains open after reasonable attempts, the note
should say what has been checked and what remains unknown.

\section{Counterexamples}

If the cited assertion appears to be false, the note should not stop at saying
that the proof cannot be formalized.  It should give the counterexample, or the
smallest relevant part of it, in ordinary mathematical notation.  The example
should be accompanied by enough verification that the reader can see both sides:
the hypotheses of the cited assertion hold, and its conclusion fails.

When feasible, the counterexample should also be formalized in \Lean{}.  This is
especially valuable when the example is finite, algebraic, computational, or
otherwise small enough that the failure can be checked without reproducing the
whole surrounding theory.  The note should then state the mathematical content
of the checked counterexample and identify the corresponding Lean declaration in
a footnote.  The Lean file is not a substitute for the prose: the prose should
still explain why the example refutes the cited assertion.

\section{Revision of a Note}

A paper-gap note may be provisional.  It may begin as soon as the mathematical
obstruction has been isolated well enough to state the question, and it may be
revised as the calculation, the blueprint, or the corresponding \Lean{}
declarations become clearer.  The first version need not know the final
classification, but it should say plainly which mathematical point is known and
which point remains unsettled.

Later revisions should not make the note into a chronological log.  They should
rewrite the document so that it remains a coherent account of the present
mathematical understanding.  If the verdict changes, the conclusion should state
the current verdict; the linked issue or pull request can preserve the earlier
discussion.

\section{Form of the Note}

Each note should stand on its own.  It should give the date, cite the relevant
source article, and provide enough traceability for the reader to locate the
original passage and the project discussion.  GitHub issues and pull requests may
be linked with \verb|\href|, and source files, line ranges, and labels should be
recorded when they help the reader check the claim.  These references should
serve the exposition rather than govern it: the main text should be organized
around the mathematical assertion and its proof.

The note should introduce its notation before using it.  Symbols for
measurements, tensor factors, approximation relations, and error parameters
should be named in prose.  If an approximation relation is state-dependent, the
state should be named, or its defining expression should be given when this can
be done briefly.  Only after the notation is in place should the note state the
assertion in the cited source, using a bibliographic citation such as
\verb|\cite[Section~...]{...}| when the section or chapter is known.

    13	\section{At a glance}
    14	\begin{itemize}
    15	  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Medium.  The source-facing statements must retain
    16	  arbitrary prime characteristic while the later Pauli basis test uses a
    17	  separately named characteristic-two specialization.
    18	  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} The remaining proofs should occupy one
    19	  algebra file of roughly 100--200 lines.
    20	  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} Mathlib supplies finite matrix algebra
    21	  and finite-field facts; the generalized Pauli definitions and their
    22	  characteristic-two specialization are project-local.
    23	  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} Unitarity of shift and phase
    24	  matrices, the $p$-th-power identity, and additive-character orthogonality.
    25	  The scope correction is tracked in
    26	  \href{https://github.com/Dengnifer/MIPStarRE-A/issues/16}{GitHub issue \#16}
    27	  and descends from \localissue{0002}.

    30	\section{Key theorem forms}
    31	Let $K$ be a finite extension of $\mathbb F_p$, let
    32	$\chi(x)=\exp(2\pi i\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb F_p}(x)/p)$, and let
    33	$a,a',b\in K^n$.  The relevant identities are
    34	\[
    35	 \tau^W(a)\tau^W(a')=\tau^W(a+a'),\qquad
    36	 \tau^W(a)^p=I,
    37	\]
    38	and
    39	\[
    40	 \tau^X(a)\tau^Z(b)=\chi(-a\mathbin{\cdot}b)
    41	 \tau^Z(b)\tau^X(a).
    42	\]
    43	The explicit shift and phase matrices are unitary. The second identity implies
    44	that every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $\tau^W(a)$ satisfies $\lambda^p=1$. If
    45	$V\leq K^n$ and $v\notin V^\perp$, Fourier cancellation takes the form
    46	\[
    47	 \mathbb E_{u\in V}\chi(u\mathbin{\cdot}v)=0.
    48	\]
    49	
    50	\section{Source and formal scope}
    51	The source defines the shift and phase matrices and states their product,
    52	$p$-th-power, unitarity, spectral, and twisted-commutation properties in
    53	\cite[lines 1056--1095]{Ji2020MIPStar}. It uses the same character for Fourier
    54	cancellation over a subspace at lines 1124--1132 and extends the twisted
    55	relation to several qudits at lines 1141--1150. These assertions depend on the
    56	characteristic $p$; they are not intrinsically binary.
    57	
    58	The formal definitions \path{primeTauShift}, \path{primeTauPhase}, and
    59	\path{primeTauObservable} use the canonical character \path{ffChar} in
    60	characteristic $p$.  Their theorem statements cover the identities above for
    61	arbitrary $p$.  The declarations whose names begin with
    62	\path{tauObservable} or use \path{phaseSign} instead specialize to
    63	$p=2$, where $\chi(x)=(-1)^{\operatorname{Tr}(x)}$.  This specialization is
    64	appropriate only for the subsequent test, whose admissible sizes satisfy
    65	$q=2^k$; it is not substituted for the general statements.
    66	
    67	The proofs can be obtained directly from the displayed matrices.  A shift is a
    68	permutation matrix, a phase matrix has diagonal entries of modulus one, and a
    69	tensor product of such matrices is unitary.  Iterating the product identity
    70	gives $\tau^W(a)^p=I$.  Applying this equality to a nonzero eigenvector gives
    71	$(\lambda^p-1)v=0$, hence $\lambda^p=1$.  Finally, when
    72	$v\notin V^\perp$, the map $u\mapsto\chi(u\cdot v)$ is a nontrivial character
    73	of the finite additive group $V$, so its average vanishes.

    75	\section{Blueprint and formalization}

    77	\path{blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex}, lines~553--633 and

    79	\leanid{primeTauPhase}, \leanid{primeTauObservable}, and the accompanying
    80	product, power, unitarity, spectral, commutation, and cancellation theorems.
    81	They quantify an arbitrary prime characteristic and use the corresponding
    82	additive character.
    83	
    84	The separately named binary declarations are used by the later QPBT chapters.
    85	They specialize the same formulas to characteristic two and are not linked as
    86	implementations of the unrestricted source nodes. Thus the blueprint, the
    87	general Lean interface, and the paper agree; the binary layer is a consumer
    88	specialization rather than a restriction of the source statement.
    89	
    90	\section{Conclusion}
    91	There is no mathematical restriction in the source-facing formal statements:
    92	they retain arbitrary prime characteristic and the corresponding canonical
    93	character.  The characteristic-two declarations are separate corollaries for
    94	the QPBT parameter regime.  The remaining work is to prove the general
    95	identities from the explicit matrices and character orthogonality; it does not
    96	require changing the binary operator definitions.

    17	\section{At a glance}
    18	
    19	\begin{itemize}
    20	  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Low.  One intermediate inequality in the source
    21	  does not follow from the canonical parameter definition, but the claimed
    22	  soundness bound follows by estimating the same term directly.

    28	  \item \textbf{Key mathematical inputs.} The function
    29	  $(\log R)^{a+b}R^{-b}$ is bounded for $R\geq 4$, and the canonical lower and
    30	  upper bounds on $m$ transfer this estimate to the third soundness term.
    31	  Tracked in
    32	  \href{https://github.com/Dengnifer/MIPStarRE-A/issues/16}{GitHub issue \#16};

    36	\section{Key theorem forms}
    37	
    38	Let $a\geq 1$ and $0<b<1$ be the universal constants in the soundness
    39	function
    40	\[
    41	  \delta_{\mathrm{qld}}(\eps,m,d,q)
    42	    = a(md)^a\bigl(\eps^b+q^{-b}+2^{-bmd}\bigr).
    43	\]
    44	For $R\geq4$, let $c$ be the least even integer at least $(a+b)/b$, set
    45	$k=c\lceil\log_2\log_2 R\rceil+1$ and $q=2^k$, and let $j$ be determined by
    46	$2^j\leq c\lceil\log_2 R\rceil+1<2^{j+1}$. The remaining canonical parameters
    47	are $m=2^j$ and $d=1$. In particular,
    48	$m\geq (c/2)\log_2 R\geq\log_2 R$. The required estimate for the third summand is
    49	\[
    50	  a m^a 2^{-bm} \leq C'(\log R)^{-b},
    51	\]
    52	for a constant $C'$ depending only on $a$ and $b$.  This estimate, together
    53	with the source bounds for the first two summands, gives the asserted
    54	polylogarithmic bound for $\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}$.
    55	
    56	\section{The source comparison}
    57	
    58	The canonical parameters are defined in \cite[lines~1503--1514]{Ji2020MIPStar},
    59	and the bound and its proof occupy lines~1520--1562. At line~1543 the proof
    60	replaces $2^{-bmd}$ by $q^{-b}$ using the assertion $k\leq m$.%
    61	\footnote{Tracked in
    62	\href{https://github.com/Dengnifer/MIPStarRE-A/issues/16}{GitHub issue \#16}.
    63	The canonical parameter definition is at
    64	\path{references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex},
    65	lines~1503--1514; the bound and its proof are at lines~1520--1562, with the
    66	disputed comparison at line~1543.}
    67	That comparison does not follow from the stated parameter choice.  For example,
    68	the allowed values $a=1$ and $b=1/2$ give $c=4$, and $R=5$ gives $k=9$ but
    69	$m=8$.  Thus the displayed justification is false even though the lemma's
    70	conclusion remains valid.
    71	
    72	The third term can instead be bounded independently of $q$.  Since $d=1$ and
    73	$m\geq (c/2)\log R\geq\log R$,
    74	\[
    75	  2^{-bm}\leq R^{-b}.
    76	\]
    77	The accompanying upper bound $m\leq 2c\log R$ therefore gives
    78	\[
    79	  a m^a2^{-bm}
    80	    \leq a(2c)^a(\log R)^aR^{-b}
    81	    = a(2c)^a\bigl((\log R)^{a+b}R^{-b}\bigr)(\log R)^{-b}.
    82	\]
    83	The parenthesized factor is bounded on $R\geq4$: it is continuous and tends
    84	to zero as $R$ tends to infinity.  Absorbing its supremum into the universal
    85	constant yields the required estimate.

    87	\section{Comparison with the blueprint and formalization}
    88	
    89	The blueprint retains the source statement and uses the direct estimate above.
    90	The formal theorem has the same hypotheses and conclusion; its docstring marks
    91	the corrected intermediate argument and cites this note.%
    92	\footnote{The formal statement is
    93	\leanid{exists\_deltaQld\_introParams\_bound} in
    94	\doclink{MIPStarRE/QPBT/Test/CanonicalParams.lean}.}
    95	
    96	\section{Conclusion}
    97	
    98	The source's comparison $k\leq m$ is false for some permitted constants and
    99	values of $R$.  It is not needed: the canonical lower bound on $m$ controls the
   100	third soundness term directly and proves the same final estimate after enlarging
   101	the universal constant.

    16	
    17	\section{At a glance}
    18	
    19	\begin{itemize}
    20	  \item \textbf{Difficulty.} Low.  The paper's global polynomial shorthand
    21	  couples two constants in a way that excludes a square-root function used
    22	  explicitly later in the same paper.
    23	  \item \textbf{Estimated weight.} The formal correction is one predicate with
    24	  separate prefactor and exponent witnesses; no theorem statement changes.
    25	  \item \textbf{Mathlib/project split.} The obstruction is elementary real
    26	  analysis.  Mathlib's real-power API will discharge concrete downstream
    27	  witnesses, while the corrected convention is project-local.
    28	  \item \textbf{Key Mathlib inputs.} The downstream witnesses use the
    29	  \path{Real.rpow} API.  The obstruction here is the elementary fact that no
    30	  constant $C>0$ can bound $\sqrt{x}$ by $C x^C$ for every $x>0$.
    31	\end{itemize}
    32	
    33	\section{Key theorem forms}
    34	
    35	The paper's shorthand asks for one universal constant $C>0$ such that
    36	\[
    37	  f(x) \leq Cx^C \qquad (x>0).
    38	\]
    39	The formal one-parameter convention instead asks for constants $A\geq1$ and
    40	$r>0$ such that
    41	\[
    42	  0\leq f(x)\leq Ax^r \qquad (x\geq0).
    43	\]
    44	This form includes $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ by taking $A=1$ and $r=1/2$.
    45	
    46	\section{The source convention}
    47	
    48	The asymptotic conventions of \cite[lines~23--29]{Ji2020MIPStar} define
    49	$f(x)=\operatorname{poly}(x)$ using the same constant as prefactor and
    50	exponent.  Later, the Pauli basis analysis explicitly obtains
    51	$\delta_{\mathrm{acom}}(\eps)=\sqrt{\eps}$ and
    52	$\delta_{\mathrm{Line}}(\eps)=\sqrt{\eps}$ at lines~508--520 and 649--676 of
    53	the chapter-14 source mirror.\footnote{The corresponding files are
    54	\path{references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex} and
    55	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex}.  The
    56	formal correction is tracked in
    57	\href{https://github.com/Dengnifer/MIPStarRE-A/issues/16}{GitHub issue \#16}
    58	and descends from \localissue{0002}.}
    59	
    60	The coupled-constant inequality cannot hold for $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$.  At $x=1$ it
    61	would imply $C\geq1$.  For such a constant,
    62	\[
    63	  \frac{\sqrt{x}}{Cx^C}=C^{-1}x^{1/2-C}
    64	\]
    65	is unbounded as $x$ decreases to zero, contradicting the proposed inequality
    66	on all positive inputs.

    70	The blueprint records only the paper's local assertions that the relevant
    71	errors are polynomial in $\eps$; those assertions include the displayed
    72	square-root choices.  The formal helper therefore separates the prefactor and

    74	\doclink{MIPStarRE/QPBT/Games/ErrorFunctions.lean}.}  This changes no
    75	source-labelled theorem and preserves the intended meaning that the error
    76	decays as a positive power of its argument.

    79	
    80	The single-constant shorthand is incompatible with the paper's own
    81	square-root error functions.  Using independent positive exponent and
    82	prefactor witnesses is a local correction to that shorthand, not an
    83	unfaithful theorem dependency.

    21	
    22	\section{At a glance}
    23	
    24	\begin{itemize}
    25	  \item \textbf{Difficulty: easy.}  The issue is a quantifier exchange between
    26	  a supremum and an attained maximum in a preliminary lemma on nonlocal games.
